{"stdout":"# Editorial playbook — AI Edge Briefing

You are producing today's edition of a daily briefing on frontier AI. The reader uses this as their single place to stay at the edge: the advances, the research, and how AI is being used for good and for harm — cyber, influence ops, military, health, science, policy. It is not a "fun uses of AI" newsletter. It is raw, factual, sourced.

The reader's standard: **every claim links to where it came from, every number is the number in the source, and nothing is written that the sources do not say.** If you cannot source it, it does not go in.

## 0. Setup

1. Work in the repo root. Determine today's date in **America/Toronto**: `TZ=America/Toronto date +%F`. That is the edition date, `DATE`.
2. `ls data/` — the previous edition tells you the cutoff. The coverage window (`WINDOW`) is from the previous edition's `generated_at` to now (if there is no previous edition, the 24 hours before now). Write it down as absolute timestamps in both UTC and ET; you will hand it to the subagents. Read the previous edition so you do not repeat it; a story already covered goes in again **only if there is a new development**, flagged `update`, and the bullets report only the new facts.
3. `node scripts/build.js --topics` — the existing topic slugs. Reuse them; only coin a new slug when nothing fits.
   `node scripts/build.js --storylines` — the open storylines (id, status, name, frame). An item that is a development in one of those arcs is **filed under it** (see §3, `storylines`). The daily never creates a storyline; the Monday Week in Review does.
4. Every day is a daily edition, Mondays included. The week in review is a separate weekly edition with its own playbook (`PROMPT-WEEK.md`) and its own routine — never part of the daily file.

## 0b. Keep your own context small — it is most of what this edition costs

Every turn you take re-sends this whole conversation. So the price of anything you pull into your context
is its size **times the number of turns that come after it** — a page you open early is paid for a hundred
times over. Measured: writing the edition costs about $3; re-reading the conversation while writing it costs
about $20. None of the rules below cost you a source, a check or an item. They stop you paying rent on text
you have already used.

1. **Write files with `Write`, and change them with `Edit`.** Never `cat > file <<'EOF'`, and never a
   `python3 -`/`node -e` script that does find-and-replace on a data file — those put the whole file, or
   whole paragraphs twice over, into the conversation as a command argument. `Edit` sends only the line that
   changes.
2. **Never print a file back out after writing it.** You know what you wrote. To check it, run the
   validator — it prints errors, not contents.
3. **Read the part you need.** `sed -n '40,80p'` over `cat` for anything long, and don't re-read a file
   that has not changed since you read it.
4. **`node scripts/fetch.js` caps its output at 12,000 characters** — the claim, the date and the figures
   are at the top of a page. Add `--full` only when you have looked and what you need is genuinely further
   down. Don't pipe it through `head` as well; the cap is already there.
5. **Let the subagents hold the raw material.** A beat opens fifty pages and hands you back a page of facts;
   that is the whole point of them. When you need a page opened and checked, and a subagent can do it,
   prefer that to opening it yourself.
6. Same rules for the subagents you launch — put a short version of this in every prompt you give them.

None of this licenses checking less. If a fact needs a source opened, open it. Verify everything §2 says to
verify. This is about what you keep afterwards, not what you look at.

## 1. Sweep the sources — four beats in parallel

Read `SOURCES.md`. Then launch **four general-purpose subagents in one message** with the Agent tool, one per beat. Give each: the `WINDOW` as absolute timestamps, its beat's source list from `SOURCES.md`, the **Sourcing rules** below verbatim, and the return format. Tell each to run many searches (15–30) and to open the listed primary sources directly. If the Agent tool is unavailable, work the four beats yourself in turn — do not skip any.

- **Beat A — Frontier models & labs · Compute, chips & infrastructure · Deployment & impact (industry, funding, labor).** SOURCES.md §1, §7, §8.
- **Beat B — Research & papers (incl. safety, alignment, evals).** SOURCES.md §2. arXiv new listings (cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CR, cs.CV, cs.RO), Hugging Face papers, alphaXiv, Nature/Science, lab research blogs, Epoch, METR, AISI, CAISI, Apollo, Redwood, Alignment Forum. Prefer papers with a notable quantitative result, from major labs/universities, or drawing significant attention. Return arXiv IDs and author institutions.
- **Beat C — Security, misuse & threat intelligence · Military, defense & geopolitics.** SOURCES.md §3, §4. AI-enabled intrusions and malware, fraud and scams, deepfakes, influence operations, surveillance, prompt injection and agent exploits, model theft / illicit distillation, bio/chem misuse reports; procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies.
- **Beat D — Health, science & medicine · Policy, regulation & law.** SOURCES.md §5, §6. Clinical results, FDA/Health Canada/WHO actions, drug discovery, AI for science, biosecurity; legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings and filings, government reports, standards — US federal and state, EU, UK, Canada, China, international bodies.

**Subagent return format** — one block per item, then a short list of rejected candidates and why:

```
SECTION: <one of the eight section names>
HEADLINE: <factual, specific, max 18 words, no hype>
PUBLISHED: <date/time and timezone exactly as the source shows it>
SOURCES: one per line — <publisher> | <exact URL> | primary or report   (only URLs actually opened or seen in search results; never constructed)
FACTS: 2–5 bullets, each a verifiable fact from a linked source, numbers/units/baselines exactly as written, naming which source
FLAGS: company-claim | single-source | preprint | update  (any that apply)
```

**Sourcing rules (give to subagents verbatim):**
1. Only include facts that appear in a source you opened (WebFetch) or in the text of a search result. No inference, speculation, predictions or "this could mean". No hype adjectives.
2. Every item links to the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page. Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, company post, government document, filing, court record) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item. Older stories qualify only if something new happened inside the window, and only the new facts are reported (flag `update`).
4. Attribute claims: "OpenAI says…", "according to The Record…". Company-reported benchmarks, user counts, revenue and capability claims get `company-claim` unless independently verified. Research that is not peer reviewed gets `preprint`.
5. Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and the comparison baseline. Do not round, convert or compute new figures.
6. If `WebFetch` refuses a page, fetch it directly with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>` — the sites we read have given permission for direct reads, and the fetcher identifies itself. Use only what the returned text actually says; if it comes back as a paywall stub, a login page or nothing usable, fall back to search-result text or another source and say in the bullet where the figures came from. Never use archive or cache sites, and never cite a URL whose content you did not see. Sites that refuse `WebFetch` are listed in SOURCES.md.
7. Skip consumer tips, "fun uses", prompt guides, listicles, opinion pieces without new facts, minor feature updates, unsourced rumours, and small funding rounds unless strategically notable (US$100M+, or a frontier lab / defense / health / security company).
8. When in doubt, leave it out.

After the beats return, run a few **gap-check searches** yourself for anything a beat may have missed (WebSearch: "AI" + Pentagon / drone; "AI" + FDA / hospital; "AI" + scam / deepfake / influence operation; "AI" + export controls / data center power; "AI" + lawsuit / ruling; plus Techmeme and Hacker News front page), restricted to the window.

## 2. Verify and select

Merge the beats' returns. De-duplicate across beats and against previous editions. Then, for each candidate:
- Open the primary source. Confirm the headline and every number/date/name you intend to use. A secondary report of a paper links the paper. A report of a court ruling links the ruling or docket where possible.
- Prefer two independent sources for anything contested, surprising, or about a specific actor (a named threat group, a company's claim about a rival, a casualty figure).
- Drop: opinion pieces without new facts, product marketing with no numbers, speculation, "could" / "may" stories, anything you cannot open, anything older than the window without a new development.
- Spot-verify: open (WebFetch, or `node scripts/fetch.js` if it refuses) the key source for every item you will mention in the summary and for every figure in the summary; confirm date, numbers and URL yourself. Remove anything you cannot confirm.
- Keep: model/system releases with benchmarks or capabilities; papers with a result (state the result); documented misuse and threat-intel reports (name actors, counts, dates); military and government procurement/deployment; clinical and scientific results; regulation, enforcement, court decisions; compute/chip/energy facts with figures; large-scale deployments and measured impacts, good or bad.

## 3. Write the edition — `data/DATE.json`

Schema (see `data/2026-09-11.json` for a full example once it exists):

```json
{
  "date": "YYYY-MM-DD",
  "edition": "daily",
  "generated_at": "<ISO-8601 UTC timestamp>",
  "window": "e.g. 10 Sep 11:00 → 11 Sep 11:00 UTC",
  "title": "The episode's name — 3 to 10 words, a statement: who did what, or what changed. No period, no colon, no figure that is not in the summary. It is read in podcast apps as 'Name [2 Oct 2026]', so it must stand alone.",
  "summary": ["paragraph 1", "paragraph 2"],
  "sections": [
    {
      "name": "<one of the eight section names below>",
      "items": [
        {
          "headline": "Specific, factual, one line — who did what, with the key number",
          "sources": [{ "name": "Anthropic", "url": "https://..." }, { "name": "Reuters", "url": "https://..." }],
          "bullets": ["What was announced/found, with numbers.", "Why it matters / what it changes.", "Caveats, what is unverified, what to watch."],
          "topics": ["anthropic", "threat-intel", "cyber-offense"],
          "storylines": ["ai-enabled-hacking"],
          "impact": "beneficial" | "harmful" | "mixed" | "neutral",
          "flags": ["company-claim" | "single-source" | "preprint" | "update"]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

1. `Frontier models & labs` — releases, capabilities, benchmarks, lab announcements, safety cases, system cards.
2. `Research & papers` — papers with results: new methods, evals, interpretability, alignment, scaling. State the result and the number.
3. `Security, misuse & threat intelligence` — threat-intel reports, documented attacks using AI, influence operations, scams/deepfakes, model vulnerabilities, prompt injection, jailbreaks, agent security.
4. `Military, defense & geopolitics` — procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies, China/US/EU competition.

8. `Deployment & impact` — large-scale rollouts, labor effects, measured societal effects, incidents, the good and the bad in practice.

OpenAI, Bartz v. Anthropic, Kadrey v. Meta, Getty v. Stability), techpolicy.press, lawfaremedia.org, brookings.edu AI, iapp.org/news/, adalovelaceinstitute.org, cdt.org, epic.org, ainowinstitute.org, futureoflife.org, politico.com/tag/artificial-intelligence, axios.com/technology/ai

NEVER use archive.org, archive.ph or any cache site. NEVER cite a URL whose content you did not actually see. If a fetch returns a paywall stub or login page, fall back to WebSearch result text or another source and say in the bullet where the figures came from. WebSearch with allowed_domains rejects reuters.com, wsj.com, nytimes.com, wired.com, theverge.com, arstechnica.com — search without the domain filter.

1. Only include facts that appear in a source you opened or in the text of a search result. No inference, speculation, predictions or "this could mean". No hype adjectives.
2. Every item links to the specific article, paper, ruling or document — never a homepage or index page. Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, FDA clearance/press release, government document, filing, court record, docket) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item.
4. Attribute claims: "the FDA says…", "according to the filing…". Company-reported clinical or capability claims get `company-claim` unless independently verified. Research not peer reviewed gets `preprint`.
5. Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units, confidence intervals and the comparison baseline. Do not round, convert or compute new figures.
6. A report of a court ruling links the ruling or docket where possible.
7. Skip opinion pieces without new facts, think-tank commentary with no new data, minor guidance restatements.
8. When in doubt, leave it out.

ALREADY COVERED YESTERDAY (2026-10-21) — do not repeat unless genuinely new inside the window, flagged `update`: Radical Numerics AI-designed phages given to a patient; two FDA-cleared pulmonary embolism models falling below clearance sensitivity across a 17-facility system; FDA digital health director saying the agency will draft generative-AI device policy after 300+ comments; OpenAI acquiring Orchestra Bio into its Rosalind suite; study finding 97.7% of AI incidents tied to US-listed issuers drew no incident-specific SEC disclosure; UK Digital and Technologies Jobs Plan (200,000 entry-level tech jobs); Clearview AI's UK Court of Appeal argument on the ICO deletion order.

KEEP YOUR OWN CONTEXT SMALL: don't print whole files back out; read only the part you need.

RETURN FORMAT — one block per item (aim for 10–18 solid candidates), then a short list of rejected candidates and why:

SECTION: <one of: Health, science & medicine | Policy, regulation & law | Frontier models & labs | Research & papers | Security, misuse & threat intelligence | Military, defense & geopolitics | Compute, chips & infrastructure | Deployment & impact>
HEADLINE: <factual, specific, max 18 words, no hype>
PUBLISHED: <date/time and timezone exactly as the source shows it>
SOURCES: one per line — <publisher> | <exact URL> | primary or report
FACTS: 2–5 bullets, each a verifiable fact from a linked source, numbers/units/baselines exactly as written, naming which source
FLAGS: company-claim | single-source | preprint | update

Run many searches. Be thorough. Factual accuracy over speed.

A Small Model Asks Better: Fine-Tuning Query Clarification for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28686
arXiv:2610.28686v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Query clarification is essential for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems that face ambiguous user queries. We consider multi-turn grounded conversational scenarios where a user query is either ill-formed or ambiguous in the context of the prior dialog or, more interestingly, it may be well-formed but when posed against retrieved documents there are multiple relevant interpretations. The task is to recognize both such cases and then generate an appropriate clarification request to the user. We present ClariEdge, a new dataset of approximately 3,900 examples that include such ambiguous queries along with negative examples that do not require clarification. We also show that a lightweight fine-tuned LoRA achieves 96.6% classification accuracy and outperforms prompted baselines of many larger models on both classification and quality of clarification generation. Our study shows that hard negatives are an essential ingredient to separate out queries that are truly ambiguous from queries that may look ambiguous but are not (i.e., can be resolved from the context). The same LoRA achieves high performance in both pre-retrieval and post-retrieval scenarios; thus, it can be used in two places in a RAG pipeline as a check before answer generation. The ClariEdge dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ibm-research/ClariEdge.

Scaling in Games: Continued Pre-Training For Embodied Agents In Diverse Virtual Worlds
https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28698
arXiv:2610.28698v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Scaling data, diversity and model capacity has improved embodied learning in physical environments, where diverse experiences remain grounded in shared physical laws. Whether these gains extend to virtual worlds with different visual styles, dynamics, controls, and objectives remains unclear. We investigate this question through a controlled study of continued pre-training (CPT) across three axes: data volume, diversity, and model size. Our 120 training configurations span four model sizes from 0.8B to 27B, six data budgets from 50 to 1,600 hours, and five mixtures ranging from Minecraft-only data to diverse multi-world corpora. We assess performance and generalization using three-level validation losses and gameplay benchmarks from in-corpus worlds to unseen worlds. Our results show: (1) more data improves in-corpus performance, diversity improves transfer to related worlds with limited gains in distant worlds, and model size improves data efficiency but generalizes worse to distant worlds under single-world training; (2) we observe an early interface phase with broad cross-world benefits and a later world phase with gains narrowed to in-corpus and related worlds, and fit an empirical scaling law relating validation loss to data volume, diversity and model size; and (3) our models are competitive with Minecraft specialists and frontier models in 3D worlds, and perform best in real-time settings. However, the limits of imitation and persistent gaps in distant worlds suggest that building generalist embodied agents requires richer training stages beyond continued pre-training.

SpecEvo: Speculative Evolution with Large Language Models for Cost-Efficient Scientific Discovery
https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28706
arXiv:2610.28706v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: LLM-driven evolutionary search is a promising paradigm for scientific discovery, but existing methods remain costly and slow, often applying expensive reasoning uniformly while underusing evidence from failed, redundant, and saturated trials. We introduce Speculative Evolution (SpecEvo), a multi-LLM framework that coordinates lightweight and frontier models through continual consolidation of search evidence. Lightweight models power both parallel Speculators, which generate and refine candidate programs, and an Advisor, which distills accumulated successes, failures, and saturated directions into persistent guidance for subsequent exploration. At sparse checkpoints, a frontier-model Navigator inspects the evolving population and intervenes through synthesis, surgical refinement, or reframing according to search stagnation. This speculate-then-consolidate workflow delegates routine exploration and evidence consolidation to inexpensive models while reserving frontier reasoning for strategic interventions whose benefits extend across many subsequent low-cost evaluations. Across 176 tasks spanning four scientific and algorithmic discovery domains, SpecEvo matches or outperforms frontier-model baselines while reducing API cost by up to 80%, achieves up to 1.5x greater evaluation efficiency than cost-efficient baselines on equation discovery, and improves over the strongest CO-Bench baseline by 3.8%. These results support trajectory-conditioned model coordination as an effective approach to cost-efficient scientific discovery.

Abstract: Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce Agent4Sci, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today's agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, Agent4Sci asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in-the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today's frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain-relevant interventions. Agent4Sci gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for-science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub (https://github.com/maszhongming/agent4sci) and Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/MingZhong/agent4sci).

https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28815
arXiv:2610.28815v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Agentic harness evolution optimizes an agent's instructions, tools, and control flow by using its task execution experiences as evolving evidence. While more evolution tasks should intuitively improve performance, our preliminary study reveals a paradoxical failure mode: the performance of existing methods degrades as the task pool expands. Our further analysis demonstrates that this degradation stems from suboptimal evidence selection during optimization, as different evidence combinations lead to substantially different evolution outcomes. To address this issue, we propose Successive Scale Racing (SSR), a framework that adaptively searches for optimal evidence combinations in each evolution round. SSR constructs diverse evidence combinations based on the corresponding task quality and coverage, and efficiently races the resulting candidate harnesses under a small compute budget. Empirically, across three distinct benchmarks, SSR achieves state-of-the-art results in all six configurations. Notably, as the task pool grows from 40 to 200, SSR steadily improves the pass rate from 64.3% to 68.3%, while the baselines' performances all drop. Furthermore, its racing mechanism identifies near-optimal candidates while reducing validation executions by 60%.

Here's a summary of the search results. The most time-sensitive item is a LiteLLM supply-chain compromise from October 21, 2026.

**LiteLLM supply-chain compromise (most urgent)**
- Malicious LiteLLM version 1.107.0 was published to PyPI on October 21, 2026, and the matching Docker images were also poisoned after attackers used stolen maintainer tokens to push trojanized wheels to PyPI and tainted Docker images. The payload is a credential stealer, and the malware runs every time Python starts on an infected machine, even if the project never uses LiteLLM.
- Wiz reported that the stolen credentials were already being used, with the attacker checking stolen AWS instance role credentials and then listing Amazon Bedrock models, a pattern consistent with LLMjacking. As of October 22, no threat actor has been publicly attributed.
- Separately, Check Point reported critical flaws in LiteLLM (CVE-2026-35029 and CVE-2026-59823) that could let low-privileged users steal credentials, and LiteLLM has addressed both.

**AI-enabled malware and stealers**
- Symantec's analysis of the Aoki stealer found that newer versions search for files tied to Claude, ChatGPT and Codex, plus tokens for tools like GitHub Copilot and Cursor.
- Microsoft's 2026 Digital Defense Report, reported October 2, says some actors have tried agentic workflows and LLM-generated code to speed up malware deployment. It also covers the s1ngularity malware, which looked for Claude Code, Gemini CLI or Amazon Q CLI on infected machines to hunt for secrets and SSH keys.
- Check Point's October 19 threat roundup noted that repeated changes in teammate behavior raised one agent's violation rate from 44% to 98% in controlled experiments.

**Other notes**
- Huntress reported at least 40 related incidents, including two confirmed infections that began through Custom GPTs. Those GPTs were used in a ClickFix campaign to deliver remote access malware.
- Unit 42 described attackers using an LLM to generate malicious scripts in the Shai-Hulud campaign. Its search metadata is unreliable, though, so I can't confirm this is a 2026 report.

The accord is titled "White House Accord on Super Intelligence, Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities" and is a one-page document (The meeting produced a one-page document).

I could not verify that second item against a primary source.

I found no evidence of a separate accord signed in October 2026, so the September 29 signing is most likely the event you're asking about.

response.result:
**Publication and incident dates**
- Article published: October 22, 2026 (the page lists "Oct 22, 2026")
- Incident date: October 21, 2026

**Exact version numbers**
- Malicious release: **1.107.0** (all seven PyPI wheels, plus Docker tags v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, main-stable)
- Recommended safe pin: **1.106.2**
- Earlier, unrelated March 2026 incident: **1.82.7** and **1.82.8**

**PyPI and Docker timeline (UTC, Oct 21, 2026)**
- 11:39: Seven wheels reached PyPI
- 11:46: Start of the window for the listed Docker images
- About 13:20: PyPI quarantined the version
- 13:23: PyPI removed the version
- 13:51: GHCR image removal
- 14:20: Docker Hub tags stopped being affected
- Socket's automated alert came about seven minutes after publication.

**Download counts**
- LiteLLM has "roughly 23 million weekly downloads." The article gives no download count for version 1.107.0 specifically.

**Payload behavior**
- Drops **cook.pth**, **cook.py** and **sitecustomize.py** into site-packages, using Python startup hooks (MITRE T1546.018), so it runs whenever an interpreter starts.
- A 16-module stealer collects cloud, Kubernetes, SSH, AI tool and browser secrets, plus LiteLLM proxy credential tables, then encrypts and posts them to a lookalike domain.
- On Linux and macOS, a second component checks GitHub hourly for remote code.
- Wiz observed the attacker validating stolen AWS instance role credentials about 4.5 hours after exfiltration, then listing Bedrock models and enumerating IAM.

**Attribution**
- No threat actor has been publicly attributed as of October 22, 2026.
- LiteLLM suspects the GitHub tokens leaked through logs from an internet-exposed internal deployment, but this is unconfirmed.
- The attack used stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from three LiteLLM engineers.
- Discovery credit: Upwind (public investigation) and Socket.

The search turned up no October 2026 Commission action specifically. The main development is the Digital Omnibus on AI, which was adopted and is now in force.

- **Status:** The amendment is Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. Sources report it was published in the Official Journal in late July and entered into force on 27 July 2026. It entered into force three days after its publication in the Official Journal. Sources differ slightly on the publication date, with one giving 24 July.
- **Origin:** The Commission proposed it on 19 November 2025 to address implementation problems, including delays in the designation of national competent authorities and conformity assessment bodies, as well as the absence of harmonized standards.
- **Main changes:** High-risk deadlines were pushed back. Standalone Annex III systems now face obligations from 2 December 2027. AI embedded in Annex I regulated products faces them from 2 August 2028. Watermarking obligations for AI-generated content will apply from 2 December 2026, earlier than the February 2027 date originally proposed.
- **Other changes:** Per one source, the amendment also introduces a targeted prohibition on AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery. Another notes that Article 50 transparency obligations are not amended by the Omnibus.
- **Guidance:** The Commission published draft high-risk classification guidelines on 19 May 2026 and final Article 50 transparency guidelines on 20 July 2026.

If you need something specific to October 2026, such as a new Commission proposal, a delegated act, or enforcement news, that would need a more targeted search.

content.title: LiteLLM 1.107.0 Compromised With A RAT InfoStealer
LiteLLM 1.107.0 Compromised: Credential Stealer
Contained: Oct 21, 2026 LiteLLM release v1.107.0 Compromised
LiteLLM attacked again: Malicious 1.107.0 wheels on PyPI and Docker Hub (October 2026)
litellm 1.107.0 Compromised on PyPI: Backdoored Wheels Drop a Credential Stealer and an Hourly Remote Code Loader - StepSecurity
Compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 on PyPI Installs a Credential Stealer and Backdoor - Real-time Open Source Software Supply Chain Security
LiteLLM Compromised, Steals Credentials
LiteLLM supply chain compromise: What you need to know
LiteLLM 1.107.0 Supply-Chain Compromise: Credential-Stealing Release Hit PyPI and Docker. Isolate, Rebuild and Rotate Now
LiteLLM 1.107.0 Malware: What Happened and What to Do

results:
The search turned up several advisories on the LiteLLM 1.107.0 compromise, but none from Socket, so I can't confirm a Socket advisory exists.

- **What happened:** The malicious release went out on October 21, 2026. The project's own incident report says the release pipeline was compromised and that the impacted releases have been pulled. All previous versions are safe, and the impacted releases have been pulled.
- **Exposure window:** Per Wiz, the malicious version was uploaded at 11:39 UTC and was quarantined on PyPI as of 13:20 UTC. Docker tags were also affected, with the image removal times differing across reports.
- **Payload:** Wiz describes a credential stealer targeting browser, cloud and AI secrets as well as a dormant C2 capability. Datadog says it installed a credential stealer that runs whenever Python starts and also contained a second-stage remote access trojan (RAT) backdoor. The malware is loaded through .pth and sitecustomize files, so nothing has to import litellm for the payload to run.
- **Stolen GitHub tokens:** Reports differ on the initial access. CellCog says an attacker used three developers' GitHub CLI tokens to repoint LiteLLM's release workflow at a lookalike repository. The project's report instead says a credential associated with a second developer account was used to satisfy the production approval gate. SafeDep rates a stolen PyPI token as a weaker fit and says the attacker could have used a compromised maintainer or bot credential, a private branch or mirror, or the reference the pipeline builds from. I didn't find a source that confirms the GitHub token claim directly, so treat it as unverified.
- **Remediation:** Rotate credentials and check for the version in lockfiles, requirements files, build logs, and caches. Mend advises checking lockfiles, requirements files and build logs for litellm 1.107.0. Chainguard says versions 1.106.2, 1.107.0rc1, and 1.107.0rc2 are clean.

content.title: The Deepfake Watchlist: Week of October 2–8, 2026
Scammers use AI to clone Florida sheriff’s captain’s voice in fake arrest warrant calls

results:
I ran one search. It turned up plenty of warnings and cases from October 2026, but no October 2026 arrests for AI voice or deepfake fraud.

- **Osceola County, Florida:** Scammers cloned a sheriff's captain's voice to make fake arrest-warrant calls. The sheriff's office estimates about 40 cases this year involve people impersonating police. A local official said that a person with some curiosity can clone a voice from about 20 seconds of audio. The sheriff's office says it will never phone someone demanding money over a warrant or missed jury duty.
- **Virtual kidnapping, California:** A Navy veteran lost $5,400 after a cloned version of her daughter's voice was used in a simulated kidnapping. Per the Resemble watchlist, no federal statute specifically covers an AI voice used to simulate a kidnapping, though the FBI has issued guidance on virtual kidnapping.
- **FBI election alert:** A secondary source says the FBI issued a warning on October 20, 2026 about AI deepfakes and voice clones aimed at voters. I could not confirm this on an FBI or official site, so treat it as unverified.
- **INTERPOL:** On October 18, 2026, INTERPOL launched a public-awareness campaign on AI deepfake fraud, part of Project SynthWave PLUS, which supports law enforcement against synthetic media threats, especially in Southeast Asia.
- **Philippines:** A deepfake investment-endorsement scheme involving a dentist was reported in October 2026. The arrests of two suspects in Angeles City happened in October 2025, not this month.
- **State roundup:** Newsweek has compiled warnings or cases on AI voice-cloning scams in Florida, Kentucky, North Carolina, Texas, California, Arizona, Michigan, and New York.

If you need a specific arrest from this month, a targeted search on local police press releases or DOJ announcements would be the next step.

response.result:
**Publication date:** October 21, 2026. The post was last updated at 20:30 UTC that day.

**Timeline (UTC, October 21, 2026)**
- **10:08:29:** GitHub branch protection rejected an unauthorized change to the private release workflow.
- **10:08:34:** A privileged developer account's credential was used to override those protections and apply the modified workflow.
- **10:46:39:** The modified workflow ran a staging build from the attacker-controlled repository Berri-AI/litellm.
- **11:08:09:** The staging run completed successfully.
- **11:08:53:** The production release pipeline began.
- **11:11:18:** A second developer account's credential was used to satisfy the production approval gate.
- **11:39:51–11:40:13:** Seven malicious litellm==1.107.0 wheels were uploaded to PyPI.
- **11:46:56:** Container publication jobs ran, and the Docker image included malicious content.
- **11:53:49–11:54:01:** A third developer account's credential was used to delete the production and staging workflow records.
- **12:09:38–12:24:52:** The unauthorized workflow revision was removed and the prior revision restored.
- **13:23:** PyPI removed litellm==1.107.0.
- **13:51:** The affected GHCR tags were found unavailable.
- **14:20:** All affected Docker Hub tags and image variants were removed or repointed to clean artifacts.

**Affected versions**
- **PyPI:** litellm==1.107.0 (all seven wheels), live from 11:39:51 to 13:23 UTC.
- **Docker Hub:** v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable, pointed to the compromised index from 11:46:56 to 14:20 UTC.
- **GHCR:** the same four tags, live from 11:46:56 UTC until unavailable by 13:51 UTC.
- The official v1.107.0 source tag in GitHub does not contain the malicious files.
- Enterprise customers using the private registry were not affected: "Enterprise Customers running the private enterprise release of LiteLLM were not impacted."

**How the attacker got access (as described; the post says some points are unconfirmed)**
- The attacker held three sets of developer GitHub CLI credentials, one of which could run workflows.
- The attacker used a token belonging to one of two GitHub organization owners to disable branch protections and force-push a change that let the releaser point to a different source repository.
- Claude Code was reported to sometimes embed a user's GitHub CLI OAuth token in response bodies. Where those bodies were logged, tokens could appear in LiteLLM logs.
- An unexpected, innocuously named user account on LiteLLM's internal deployment was exposed to the public internet. The team believes the attacker used tokens from that deployment's logs.
- How the attacker reached the internal deployment is not confirmed. The team suspects a recently patched vulnerability.

**Download and impact numbers:** The post does not include download counts or the number of affected users or environments.

**Remediation**

For affected users:
- Do not start with `pip install`, since any Python start in an affected environment reruns the malicious files.
- Delete `cook.pth`, `cook.py`, `sitecustomize.py`, and matching `__pycache__/cook*.pyc` and `sitecustomize*.pyc` from every affected site-packages.
- Kill the detached Python daemon holding `/tmp/remote_code_loader.lock`.
- Reinstall pinned to litellm==1.106.2. Rebuilding images and venvs from scratch is preferred.
- Assume exfiltration if 1.107.0 was installed on a host with outbound internet: "If 1.107.0 was ever installed on a host with outbound internet, assume the exfil succeeded."
- Rotate credentials the host could reach: the instance or task IAM role, every provider key in the proxy DB, master and virtual keys, the `DATABASE_URL` password, and any secret in the environment of processes on the host.
- Check CloudTrail for `GetCallerIdentity` from the instance role around install time, and for use of its credentials from outside your infrastructure.

Indicators to search for: `litellm-1.107.0.dist-info`, `cook.pth`, and `sitecustomize.py`. Finding one confirms exposure, but not finding one does not prove a system is clean.

For LiteLLM: the team removed the compromised packages from PyPI and revoked maintainer credentials down to the minimum needed while the investigation continues.

input.prompt: Extract publication date, timeline with UTC times, what the stealer collects, the Bedrock/LLMjacking observation, and exact numbers.

response.result:
**Publication date:** October 21, 2026

**Timeline (UTC, October 21)**

- **08:56–10:46:** The attacker pushed 10 commits to a hyphenated lookalike of BerriAI's repo. The first three, pushed within two minutes, added the persistence files. Four bumped the version to 1.107.0. After a 39-minute gap, two commits added a directive that bundled the malware into the wheel. A final commit, 58 minutes later and unsigned, added the file to the Dockerfiles.
- **11:39:** Malicious LiteLLM 1.107.0 was uploaded to PyPI.
- **13:20:** The PyPI release was quarantined.
- **~13:53:** Docker images on GHCR and Docker Hub were removed.
- **13:30:** GitHub took down the lookalike repo.
- **16:20–17:01:** Stolen AWS instance role credentials were validated, about 4.5 hours after exfiltration began.
- **Later:** The article was updated multiple times, including a LiteLLM root-cause statement. The safe version is v1.106.2.

**What the stealer collects** (a 16-module credential stealer named `privcollect`)

- **Browsers:** Credentials and cookies from Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari.
- **AWS:** Credentials from `~/.aws/`, environment variables, and EC2/ECS instance metadata (IMDS).
- **GCP:** Service account keys and application default credentials.
- **Azure:** Tokens from the CLI cache.
- **AI services:** API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere, and other LLM providers, from environment variables or config files.
- **Other:** SSH private keys, GPG keys, and shell history.
- **LiteLLM database:** Queries `LiteLLM_CredentialsTable` directly (LIMIT 500) to pull upstream provider credentials.
- **Exfiltration:** Data is encrypted with AES-256-CBC (key wrapped with RSA-4096) and sent via HTTP POST to `www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck`, a lookalike domain.

**Bedrock/LLMjacking observation**

- Between 16:20 and 17:01 UTC, the attacker validated AWS instance role credentials harvested from compromised CI runners and Kubernetes nodes across multiple environments.
- Each credential was checked with `sts:GetCallerIdentity`, then `bedrock:ListFoundationModels` and a `ListModels` call. Wiz says this matches LLMjacking.
- In a small number of environments, the attacker also enumerated IAM (`ListRoles`, `ListUsers`, `ListAccessKeys`) and ran general discovery (`ListAccounts`, `DescribeTrails`).

**Key numbers**

- Malicious version: 1.107.0
- Attacker commits: 10 (the first nine signed by GitHub)
- Stealer modules: 16
- Stealer payload size: 22,252 bytes (`cook.py`)
- Backdoor loader size: 25,509 bytes (`sitecustomize.py`)
- Encryption: AES-256-CBC, RSA-4096 key wrapping
- Database query limit: 500 rows
- Time from exfiltration to credential abuse: ~4.5 hours

2610.28891 | Thu, 22 Oct 2026 00:00:00 -0400 | Fig: Automated Multiagent Behavior Elicitor
AUTH: Anrui Gu, Zhichao Wang, Nicolai Ouporov
Abstract: Many social evaluations for multiagent systems study behaviors as they emerge from environments instead of systematically intervening in the environment to elicit such behaviors. We introduce Fig (Finding Interactions in Games), an agentic system that performs targeted elicitation interventions on game environments. It takes a natural language behavior description, decomposes it into sub-behaviors, generates new social games or selects existing ones, and executes single or combined interventions to the games' engine, opponents, instructions, and context. To evaluate model behavior, it combines built-in mechanical checks and synthetic rubric judgments. We validate the interventions, generated games, and evaluation mechanisms via human review. Models attempt the target behavior in 45.2% of episodes on average for valid scenarios generated by Fig for six test behaviors -- cooperation, exploitation, deception, covert coordination, betrayal, and sabotage. For game-behavior pairs with available controls, Fig's interventions increase attempt rates by 10.9% on average compared to m
2610.28982 | Thu, 22 Oct 2026 00:00:00 -0400 | Behavior Beyond Text: Evaluating Refusal Transfer Failure in LLM Agents
AUTH: Ekagra Gupta, Raj Saha, Aniekan-Abasi Inyang, Adam Al Gharib
Abstract: While large language models are increasingly deployed as tool-calling agents, their safety evaluations still focus primarily on their ability to refuse harmful requests in text. We investigate whether the refusal behavior in text transfers to tool use. We construct a benchmark of 2,304 prompts across four domains, consisting of matched triplets that present the same harmful or benign request in text-only, standard tool-enabled, and adversarially framed tool-enabled settings. We then assess tool-call safety using 20 predefined forbidden actions. Testing five models of varying sizes and families, we find that requests refused in text frequently result in unsafe tool calls. Under standard tool-enabled prompting, this divergence occurs for 10-52 percent of harmful requests refused in chat. #
Executive Summary

- Wiz Research uncovered multiple critical vulnerabilities in core PHP, a popular general-purpose scripting language that powers 70% of all websites in the world. Successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them.

- PHP is a backbone of the web: it’s the programming language powering WordPress, Joomla, Drupal, Wikipedia’s MediaWiki, and many others.

- These vulnerabilities include memory disclosure and unauthenticated remote code execution in PHP itself, independent of the application running on top of it , putting every affected website in immediate risk.

- Every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, going back to version 5.4. Attackers can exploit them remotely, in some cases fairly easily. Immediate patching is strongly advised.

- On October 21, 2026, PHP released the patch fixing multiple memory-safety vulnerabilities in the core engine.

- These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history. The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.

#
Overview
In this post, we explain how frontier AI helped us find and fix vulnerabilities that had remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade. The issues described below all stem from key architecture decisions, some made over a decade ago, and were grouped under two CVEs, with severity reaching CVSS 9.2. The work grew into a cross-industry effort to protect customers, find variants, deploy detections and mitigations, and verify a patch in time for coordinated disclosure.
Nearly every PHP version is affected by at least one of these issues, including releases dating back to PHP 5.4. The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory. That memory may contain passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and certificates belonging to other requests or the server itself.
PHP is the programming language behind much of the web, powering WordPress, Drupal and MediaWiki, the software that runs Wikipedia. A flaw in its core engine can affect websites across this ecosystem, even when their own application code is secure.
Some vulnerabilities become turning points because they challenge fundamental assumptions about security. In 2014, Heartbleed exposed the fragility of shared infrastructure securing the internet. In 2021, Log4Shell revealed how deeply embedded software dependencies could create widespread exposure that organizations struggled to identify. We believe PHP2Shell could mark a similar turning point for the AI era, illustrating how AI can change the practical exploitability of longstanding vulnerabilities. Building the exploit required chaining multiple flaws and adapting to each target’s memory layout through repeated testing and debugging. Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours. As the time and expertise required for this work decrease, complexity may no longer provide a meaningful barrier, changing how we define what is vulnerable in practice.
Wiz Research would like to thank the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI for their work on discovery, coordination and patch verification. OpenAI and Calif also published blogs containing details on the vulnerability – its history, technical details, and insight into the disclosure process. PHP posted as well.
We’d also like to express our sincere gratitude towards Automattic, Akamai, AWS, Cloudflare , Fastly , Google , Imperva, Microsoft, Vercel , and many others, for helping prepare guidance and out-of-the-box mitigations for customers who cannot apply the patch immediately.

The Vulnerabilities
All of the disclosed vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues that stem from bugs in how PHP handles fatal errors while processing requests, particularly out-of-memory errors. These bugs can leave a corrupted internal PHP state behind after a request ends unexpectedly. A later request or worker can reuse that stale state, leading to memory disclosure or corruption.

# News Archive - 2026

Here are the most important news items we have published in 2026 on PHP.net.

PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 fix two critical vulnerabilities that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately.

Who is at risk: all PHP installations serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. We consider the risk highest for mod_php, with a demonstrated exploit where an unauthenticated request can trigger the attack before any application code runs.

The vulnerabilities:

- RCE via OOM corruption , CVE-2026-109618 (GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w ): out-of-memory
handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat the invalid data as valid.

- RCE via stale global state , CVE-2026-109619 (GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp ): request-owned
internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed. A later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal initialization resets it.

How to update:

- Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35. Source downloads are on our downloads page . Windows source and binaries are on the same page .

- Linux distributions and LTS vendors received the patches in advance, so check your vendor for updated packages.

- PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive updates from the PHP project. Some distributions and LTS vendors provide backported fixes, so contact your vendor for details, or upgrade to a supported version.

- If you rely on the volunteer-maintained rpms.remirepo.net , we urge you to switch to distribution packages or build from source, so you can immediately apply updates. The repo will not have updates today.

- Given the severity of these vulnerabilities, the PHP security team provided minimal source-backports for PHP 7.4 , PHP 8.0 , and PHP 8.1 to help people building from source or without access to an LTS vendor.

If you cannot update immediately: while only an update is a complete solution, the following measures reduce exposure to specific attack paths but do not make an installation safe.

RCE via OOM corruption (CVE-2026-109618):

- Set memory_limit=-1 , preferably in a way applications can't override, such as php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration, and check that no pool, directory or application setting puts a finite limit back. This removes the controllable PHP memory limit failure, but an underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path.

- Set a low post_max_size . For applications that don't require file uploads, set post_max_size = 8M . If file uploads are necessary, set post_max_size = 32M . Keep upload_max_filesize below post_max_size .

content.title: Florida AG sues OpenAI, seeks to hold CEO Altman personally liable for alleged harms
Florida AG seeks to halt OpenAI development until safe for general public
Florida Attorney General seeks emergency order to restrict ChatGPT, cites harm to minors
Florida seeks injunction to halt OpenAI model development
Attorney General James Uthmeier Files First-in-the-Nation State-Led Lawsuit Against OpenAI, CEO Sam Altman for Deceptive Practices and Harms to Floridians
Florida AG files to block ChatGPT development and place restrictions on OpenAI • Florida Phoenix
From Theory to Docket: The Trend Line in Chatbot Liability
Florida AG asks judge to block minors from ChatGPT, impose sweeping OpenAI restrictions
Florida Attorney General seeks court injunction against OpenAI's ChatGPT

results:
Florida filed a lawsuit against OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman on June 1, 2026, and later sought a temporary injunction.

- **The lawsuit:** Attorney General James Uthmeier sued in state court, claiming OpenAI released ChatGPT without adequate safeguards and marketed it to the public, including children, while downplaying risks. The company is accused of violating Florida's deceptive and unfair trade practices law. The complaint includes ten counts, including gross negligence, product liability, fraudulent misrepresentation, and public nuisance. Florida also seeks to hold Altman personally liable. The office argues he is responsible for harm to Florida residents because of his conduct as CEO.
- **Alleged harms:** The complaint links ChatGPT to violent incidents, including the April 2025 Florida State University shooting. It also alleges harm to minors, such as data collection without meaningful parental oversight, and addiction.
- **Injunction request:** On September 28, Uthmeier filed a motion in Highlands County Circuit Court seeking a temporary injunction. It asks the court to temporarily bar OpenAI from developing new AI models without independent third-party safeguards and approval. Other requests include blocking ChatGPT for minors in Florida and limiting how the product is marketed. State prosecutors also opened a criminal investigation into OpenAI's conduct in April 2026.
- **Significance:** Florida is described as the first-in-the-nation state-led lawsuit against OpenAI and its CEO. Other states, including Kentucky, Pennsylvania, and Texas, are also using existing consumer protection statutes, not new AI laws, to bring cases.

I have not checked whether the court has ruled on the injunction motion, so the status may have changed since these reports.

results:
The October 21, 2026 hearing appears to have taken place. Sources differ on some background details, so treat the specifics below with care.

- **Hearing:** Cross-motions for summary judgment are fully briefed, with Anthropic's reply filed September 8, 2026, and the hearing set for October 21, 2026. A Courthouse News report describes the hearing on cross-motions for summary judgment, where publisher counsel argued that Claude reproduces copyrighted material, sometimes verbatim.
- **Anthropic's position:** Anthropic argues that training Claude on copyrighted song lyrics is transformative fair use under Section 107 and that the publishers' DMCA Section 1202 claim fails as a matter of law. Per Courthouse News, Anthropic also says Claude users prompt the chatbot to produce lyrics and the company only has secondary liability.
- **Publishers' position:** Universal Music Publishing Group, Concord, and ABKCO filed a partial summary judgment motion urging Judge Eumi Lee to reject the fair use defense before trial.
- **Judge and ruling:** US District Judge Eumi Lee heard arguments on competing motions in San Jose. I found no report of a ruling yet. The Yahoo/Hollywood Reporter item about the publishers losing a preliminary injunction bid dates from an earlier stage of the case, not this hearing.
- **Caveats:** The Exhibit AI summary contains some background details (such as filing dates and the case's procedural history) that conflict with other sources, so verify those against the docket. The case number cited by most sources is 5:24-cv-03811-EKL-SVK.

The search didn't turn up OpenAI's own blog post or any "five-stage" disclosure framework, so I can't confirm that part of your query. The coverage that did come back is consistent on the main points, with a few date discrepancies.

- **What it is:** Researchers from Wiz, OpenAI, and Calif jointly disclosed two PHP memory-safety flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, which together are called php2shell. The vulnerabilities affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later, and successful exploitation can lead to full remote code execution without authentication.
- **OpenAI's role:** OpenAI's President Greg Brockman said the company led a two-month coalition under the "Patch the Planet" initiative to fix the PHP2Shell vulnerability. Reports credit GPT-5.6 Sol with helping find the bugs. Calif's first version was found using it, and OpenAI found a more complete version in September.
- **Discovery dates conflict:** One outlet says the PHP2Shell vulnerability was first identified in July 2026 by a security firm called Calif, while another says Security firm Calif discovered a version of the vulnerability in August. Fortune reports that the Wiz team identified the first issue on Aug. 19.
- **Disclosure and patch:** PHP shipped emergency security updates on Wednesday. They fix two critical flaws that let an unauthenticated attacker run code on almost any server running the language. Cloudflare says its WAF protections were deployed about 9 hours ahead of public disclosure.
- **Impact:** The disclosure prompted some government websites in Europe to go offline as companies updated their systems, according to Reuters. Coverage also notes that whether php2shell has actually been exploited in the wild at scale remains unconfirmed.
- **Aardvark:** The only Aardvark result is older coverage of OpenAI's autonomous security agent, which is now in private beta. Nothing I found links it directly to php2shell.

input.prompt: Give the exact publication date and time, author, and the key facts: what was argued, by whom, judge name, case number, court, specific quotes and numbers.

response.result:
**Publication:** October 21, 2026, by Carly Nairn (Courthouse News Service). The article doesn't give a time.

**Court and judge:** U.S. District Judge Eumi Lee. The hearing was in San Jose, Calif. The article doesn't name the court further and gives no case number.

**Parties:** Concord Music Group, Capitol CMG, Universal Music, Songs of Universal, Polygram Publishing, and Abkco Music sued Anthropic in October 2023. They want Anthropic to license copyrighted works it uses.

**Hearing:** Cross-motions for summary judgment.
- Plaintiffs' attorney Matthew Oppenheim argued Claude reproduces copyrighted lyrics, sometimes verbatim. He targeted derivative works and "synthetic" songs that compete with human artists. He said, "It couldn't do it if it didn't have the lyrics in the database."
- Oppenheim also said, "Copyright is a monopoly by nature," in response to Judge Lee's question about whether the labels' position would give publishers a monopoly over lyrics.
- Anthropic attorney Sonal Mehta argued Anthropic has only secondary liability because users prompt the lyrics or songs. She said the synthetic songs are new, copyrightable material and that "There isn't anything in the record that shows doom for the music industry."
- The labels also allege Anthropic removes content management information to conceal infringement.

**Prior rulings:**
- January 2025: Judge Lee ordered Anthropic to keep existing copyright guardrails for Claude's inputs and outputs and apply them to future models. She did not broadly halt training on copyrighted lyrics.
- Last October (2025): She denied Anthropic's motion to dismiss, reasoning that Anthropic earns revenue each time users submit requests for lyrics and each time its API generates output relying on them.

**Outcome:** Judge Lee took the summary judgment motions under submission and did not indicate her views.

**Other Anthropic litigation:** The article mentions a 2025 Reddit lawsuit over training data and a $1.5 billion settlement with book authors, described as the largest settlement in U.S. copyright case history.

2610.28797 | Thu, 22 Oct 2026 00:00:00 -0400 | CALLIOPE: Private Insights into AI Use, Without Embeddings
AUTH: Edith Cohen, Vadym Doroshenko, Badih Ghazi, Charlie Harrison, Pritish Kamath, Alexander Knop, Ravi Kumar, Ethan Leeman, Pasin Manurangsi, Mikhail Pravilov, Adam Sealfon, Yurii Sushko, Marika Swanberg, Chiyuan Zhang
Abstract: We introduce CALLIOPE, a top-down framework for discovering topic hierarchies in large corpora of unstructured data (e.g., LLM conversations), while supporting differential privacy (DP). Unlike traditional and even recent LLM-augmented approaches that ultimately rely on clustering vector embeddings, our framework leverages LLM capabilities directly for the entire pipeline. Experiments demonstrate that this approach provides better utility over existing (embedding-based) methods in the DP setting, especially in the high privacy regime. We evaluate the quality of CALLIOPE outputs using a variety of traditionally studied clustering metrics, as well as some novel utility metrics that we introduce.

2610.29927 | Thu, 22 Oct 2026 00:00:00 -0400 | Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty
AUTH: Yifan Sun, Naicheng Yu, Jiawen Gong, Jingyan Shen, Huan Zhang
Abstract: A benchmark is not merely a collection of test questions; it naturally induces an empirical measure over difficulty. In this work, we develop this measure-based view of benchmark evaluation. This perspective allows us to identify and formalize two central failure modes: measure mismatch, where the benchmark difficulty distribution differs from the intended difficulty distribution, and coverage gaps, where uncovered regions along the difficulty axis prevent benchmarks from detecting meaningful localized training progress. We propose two diagnostic metrics that capture these two failure modes and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we analyze 25 popular benchmarks spanning 7 domains using carefully estimated item difficulties. Our results show that many benchmarks implicitly overweight certain difficulty regions, so their leaderboard conclusions should be interpreted with caution; others leave substantial portions of the difficulty axis uncovered, limiting their ability to monitor the model improvement process. Finally, we turn diagnosis into action by intro

Abstract: Can LLM agents make contributions to frontier computer science R&D? We introduce FrontierCS 2, a benchmark of 48 open-ended tasks. We take a paper and the code its authors released and delete the paper's contribution. The deleted code becomes the human reference that sets the bar. Earlier open-ended benchmarks give each agent a problem statement and grade one program after the run. FrontierCS 2 places the agent inside a research environment. The agent inherits a working repository and may submit a patch at any point. For each patch, a judge returns a development-suite score but keeps the evaluator, the held-out final suite and the reference private, and grades the final submission on that suite against the reference. The tasks span 13 domains, from machine-learning systems and high-performance computing to databases, security and robotics. Beyond these 48 tasks, FrontierCS 2 keeps a private set of more than 100 tasks, to be announced in the future. We evaluate 12 agents. The best one is Claude Opus 5.5, passing 58% of its runs. Cloudflare deploys protections against php2shell vulnerability | Cloudflare Blog

Skip to content

Today, Calif.io, Wiz, OpenAI and Quarkslab disclosed two vulnerabilities in PHP, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and known as php2shell . The vulnerabilities affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later and they may allow an attacker to cause denial of service, remote code execution, and data exposure when an application processes specially crafted HTTP traffic.
Cloudflare has been part of a coordinated effort to deploy mitigations to protect the Internet, working with PHP foundation , OpenAI and Wiz among others. Cloudflare has developed and deployed web application firewall (WAF) protections since early October 2026, which were deployed about 9 hours ahead of public disclosure. Starting on October 21 3:02 am UTC, Cloudflare customers using our free or paid WAF were protected by default against php2shell.
Cloudflare successfully deployed multiple mitigations for all its customers while the vulnerability was leaked before the official release date and we observed attack traffic targeting our customers. We observed how attackers were mutating the attack payload to try to bypass our protections by tracking the volume of matches and cross-referencing with the rule logic.
Protecting against php2shell required more than standard request-based rules. Request data alone does not always provide enough evidence to distinguish an exploit from legitimate traffic. The origin’s response adds context, helping identify whether an exploit succeeded while reducing the risk of false positives.
To deliver this protection, we developed full transaction detection, a new Cloudflare WAF capability that combines signals from the request and response within the same HTTP transaction. Response rules can then block a matching origin response before it reaches the requester. The php2shell protections are the first managed detections we have released using this capability.
Customers should patch their PHP repos even with WAF protections providing an additional layer of defense-in-depth mitigation. Our security analysts continue monitoring attack activity and update the rules when and if new techniques and variations emerge in the hours and days ahead. You can track new rules in the changelog .
The protections are available and deployed automatically on all plans with WAF deployed, including Free users.

# What we know about the vulnerabilities
PHP is used by almost 70% of websites . The php2shell vulnerabilities affect the PHP runtime itself and can allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Because PHP underpins widely used platforms such as WordPress and Magento, these flaws could potentially affect a large number of applications across the Internet.
The two vulnerabilities involve how PHP handles memory when something goes wrong while processing a HTTP request. Normally, PHP allocates memory to store the data it needs to process a request, then releases it when that work finishes. If processing stops unexpectedly, for example because it runs out of memory, PHP fails to clean up the memory safely. These vulnerabilities arise when PHP handles an error and then tries to use data that was not fully set up or memory that has already been released.
An attacker can send specially crafted HTTP requests to trigger these conditions. Large requests are one way to put memory under pressure, but the problem goes beyond consuming server resources. By manipulating the data PHP encounters in this invalid memory, an attacker may be able to crash a PHP process, expose sensitive information, or execute code provided by the attacker.
The two vulnerabilities differ in when the unsafe memory access happens:
Vulnerability
What goes wrong

CVE-2026-109618
PHP runs out of memory and interrupts its work before some internal data has been properly initialized. During cleanup of that request, PHP may use this unfinished data as though it were valid.

CVE-2026-109619
A fatal error interrupts a request, leaving PHP holding references to memory that is released when the request ends. When the same PHP process handles a later request, it may follow those outdated references and access memory that is no longer valid and expose sensitive data.

# Alignment Science Blog

# Articles

October 2026

# Red-Teaming Auto Mode: Improving Blocking Classifiers Against Malign Coding Agents

We red-team production blocking monitors (Auto Mode in Claude Code, Guardian in OpenAI's Codex) with
an adversarial agent in an experimental setting with the objective of improving the safety of coding
agents.
October 2026

# Reducing Reward Hacking by Localizing Bad Behavior Instead of Penalizing It

When a model is caught cheating on a task during training, we confine its learning to a separate
set of parameters. After training, we delete those parameters.

# Training Alignment Auditors via Reinforcement Learning

We train LLMs to investigate target models with hidden behaviors planted in their system prompt. A
trained Haiku 4.5 policy matches Opus 4.6 on held-out evaluations for auditing quality and
generalizes to harder fine-tuned targets in a different scaffold.

August 2026

# Training a Misaligned Reward Seeker

Qi,* Wright, MacDiarmid, Hubinger, 2026

To better understand the impact of reward hacking on model behavior, we trained an Opus-class model with large-scale RL on many production environments vulnerable to reward hacks. We consider this a plausible proxy for what a real training run might look like had we not invested significant effort into preventing and detecting reward hacking in our normal training runs. Our results show that a high rate of reward hacking during RL can cause models to be willing to perform long sequences of harmful real-world actions in pursuit of task success.

# Automated Researchers Can Mitigate Well-Characterized Alignment Failures

Across 10 common alignment failures, the strongest technique our automated alignment researchers
discover significantly mitigates the targeted failures and generalizes out of distribution. Our
findings suggest that automating measurable alignment research may already be practical, rather
than years away.

We introduce TASTE, a benchmark measuring how well models can judge AI safety research proposals
against the preferences of experienced researchers.

# Meta says Muse has over 10M users, with shopping a top activity

Sarah Perez

2:14 PM PDT · October 21, 2026

Meta said during its third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday that its AI app Muse has been adopted by more than 10 million users, confirming estimates released earlier this week by market intelligence firm Sensor Tower.

But it is how people are using it and how much they’re spending that has caught CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s attention. Zuckerberg said about 25% of people who set up Muse now use it daily, helping improve retention.

He also shared that over a quarter of Muse’s engaged users who were shopping via the AI agent had an average purchase size of over $200, which was surprising even to industry insiders.

“Plaid told us that they hadn’t seen activity like they’re seeing with their connector on any other service before,” Zuckerberg said, referring to the financial technology company that connects payment apps to customers’ bank accounts. Muse uses Plaid’s connector to enable agentic shopping.

Beyond shopping, Zuckerberg said other popular uses for Muse include personal productivity tasks, such as connecting the AI agent to users’ email or calendars. The exec stressed that this indicates users trusted Muse’s security setup, which includes a feature called “Muse Secure VM” designed to protect their data and privacy. He also mentioned that the forthcoming “Muse Confidential VM” will prevent even Meta from seeing users’ content.

Now that Muse has achieved “product-market fit,” Zuckerberg said Meta’s focus will shift to scaling the AI agent, increasing revenue, and optimizing its compute costs. Remarkably, the tech company is forecasting that Muse will eventually bring in more revenue per user than its “family of apps” users do today — meaning its users on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger. Currently, that figure is around “several hundreds of dollars annually,” Zuckerberg said.

Meta has said it ultimately intends to monetize Muse by keeping it free for most users but keeping a percentage of the commerce taking place on the platform. Power users who want access to the most advanced AI models or more tokens will also have to pay.

Zuckerberg also noted that Meta believes Muse will be profitable after it scales.

“On the compute side, we are building out the capacity to serve more than a billion people over the next few years,” he told bankers and analysts on the Q3 earnings call. “In the near term, Muse is very compute-intensive to run, but we expect to improve its cost efficiency by more than 10x in the next year, which will enable it to be profitable once the revenue lines are at scale.”

Muse will also play a central role in Meta’s smart glasses strategy. Reality Labs, the division responsible for smart glasses, VR, and the metaverse, is still losing billions. However, the division’s losses are expected to improve from $19.1 billion in 2025 to $15 billion this year.

Beyond scaling and supporting its hardware strategy, Zuckerberg teased the company’s plans for something he called the “Muse network.” He described this as taking Muse from a “single-player game” to one where “your Muses can work with your friends’ and your families’ [Muses].”

“And if you want to buy something, it’s not just navigating to that business’s website; it’s talking to their agent,” he added.

# Recursive launches Flint, a laptop coding model it says was largely built by AI

Aditya Mehta

1:27 PM PDT · October 21, 2026

Recursive , an AI startup founded last year, is starting to live up to its name. The company, which is trying to build AI that can improve itself, released its first model, Flint , on Wednesday. Flint is a free coding model that can run on a laptop and was built largely with the help of AI.

Recursive’s automated research system, which it calls the Eureka Machine, helped with nearly every step of Flint’s development, the company says. That let a small team build the model from scratch in under four months.

Flint is an early public test of recursive self-improvement: the idea that AI can build better AI, which in turn builds even better AI. It’s also one of the most debated ideas in the industry. Some researchers fear that AI improving itself could slip out of human control. For now, Recursive’s version is more limited: an AI research assistant overseen by people that produced a model small enough for a laptop.

The company emerged from stealth in May with $650 million in funding at a $4.65 billion valuation, from backers including GV, Nvidia, and AMD Ventures. Recursive is led by CEO Richard Socher, Salesforce’s former chief scientist.

Because Flint runs on a user’s own computer rather than a company’s cloud servers, developers can use it offline, keep their code private, and avoid the usage fees that AI cloud services charge based on how much text the model processes. The model is free to download on Hugging Face, the popular site for sharing AI models, under the Apache 2.0 license, an open source license that allows free use and modification.

Flint is a mixture-of-experts model, meaning it uses only a small slice of itself for any given task: just 2.5 billion of its 40 billion settings, known as parameters, at a time. That makes it light enough for an ordinary laptop and far smaller than Meta’s Muse Spark Open , an open model built for Macs that was released last week. Muse Spark Open uses 816 billion parameters and needs at least a terabyte of memory.

Flint is also fast. In Recursive’s tests, it generated about 131 tokens (chunks of text) per second on a MacBook Pro with Apple’s M4 Pro chip — roughly twice the 58 to 69 tokens per second that similar models managed on the same machine, including Google’s Gemma 4 and Nvidia’s Nemotron 3.5 Lightning. On Nvidia’s RTX Spark, Flint topped 150 tokens per second.

On SWE-Bench Verified, a benchmark that measures how well AI can fix real-world software bugs, Flint outperformed other models under 50 billion parameters. On Recursive’s own average across six tests, only one model, Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 27B, scored higher than Flint.

The company acknowledged that Flint would need more guidance than the big paid coding assistants and suggested breaking large tasks into smaller steps. Still, early reviews were positive. Wired’s Will Knight used Flint on a Mac with 48GB of memory to build several small programs, including a to-do list app and a tool that scours the web for research. He found that smaller coding models often ran into errors or were slow compared to Claude or Codex, but Flint nailed his coding requests every time.

The Eureka Machine comes up with ideas, runs experiments, and uses the results to decide what to try next. According to the company’s launch video , it contributed to nearly every part of building Flint, from pretraining to post-training and inference.

Recursive said that Eureka’s contributions include a sparser model shape, low-bit training that shrank Flint by 71% with almost no loss in quality and custom kernels, which are specialized programs that speed up the underlying computations.

Recursive didn’t say how much time the Eureka Machine saved its researchers, but it’s not alone in leaning on AI to do research. OpenAI said last month that by mid-August, its AI agents were logging 3.1 workdays for every one worked by a human researcher.

If Recursive’s bet pays off, each new model should be able to take on longer stretches of work without human help. The company previously told TechCrunch that its $410 million compute deal with Amazon Web Services in June was “less about headcount and more about agent count.”

The longer-term goal, Socher told Wired, is for the Eureka Machine to achieve full recursive self-improvement, with humans overseeing the process and able to stop it if something goes wrong. Recursive says each new model should make the Eureka Machine a better researcher, helping it build the next one faster.
