# Red-Teaming Auto Mode: Improving Blocking Classifiers Against Malign Coding Agents

Alex Remedios 1* , Simon Storf 1* September 22, 2026

Fabien Roger 2 , John Hughes 2

1 Anthropic Fellows Program; 2 Anthropic; * Primary contributors. Name order randomised.

tl;dr
We red-team production blocking monitors (Auto Mode in Claude Code, Guardian in OpenAI's Codex) with an adversarial agent in an experimental setting with the objective of improving the safety of coding agents. Our most effective attack strategies bypass the monitor using agent-generated prompt injection against the monitor, multi-agent attacks, or malicious compaction. We attempt to improve the robustness of auto-mode by improving tool coverage, transcript formatting and using an agentic monitor stage. We find that robustly preventing multi-context attacks at an acceptable cost remains an open problem.

📝 Paper , 💻 Code

Research done as part of the Anthropic Fellows Program .

# Introduction

Coding agents can now run for days with little or no human involvement, completing software tasks end to end ( Kwa et al., 2026 ). That autonomy requires broad access to the environment: a shell, the filesystem, credentials, and the network. This poses the risk of an agent taking dangerous actions with its access to the user's system.

Most dangerous actions by agents to date have been the result of over-eagerness while completing a task. However, persistent adversarial agents attempting to attack the infrastructure hosting them are an emerging threat, as demonstrated by the recent Hugging Face incident and related events ( OpenAI , Anthropic , AISI ).

Blocking monitors ( Lindner et al., 2025 ; Stickland et al., 2025 ) have been developed and tested for the over-eagerness failure mode. They check each action (e.g. a bash command) against a separate LLM-based classifier, and block unsafe actions, after which the agent proposes a new action. Claude's Auto Mode and Codex's Guardian are the most widely used versions of these in production currently. The common features of these two monitors are (a) they evaluate actions against a set of rules, (b) they can block with a reason that is fed back to the agent, and (c) they terminate a session after exceeding some number of blocks.

In this work we study the robustness of blocking monitors against the threat of persistent adversarial agents. We focus on catastrophic harms that can't be reversed and for which asynchronous monitoring ( Lindner et al., 2025 ) is insufficient. These include exfiltration of data, their own model weights in the most extreme case, and evasion of the blocking monitor by disabling it or creating new unmonitored agents. The four main attack types we study are monitor injection, multi-context attacks, coverage gaps and policy failures.

Production monitors fail to block over 55% of attacks. Each trial tests the ability of an Opus 5 red-team agent to complete a side task before incurring 20 blocks from the monitor, and we show average success rate across multiple evaluation settings and side tasks. In some trials the red-team agent has affordances such as details of the monitor internals. Error bars on the means are 95% confidence intervals.

# Training Alignment Auditors via Reinforcement Learning

Paul Rosu October 15, 2026

Rowan Wang

tl;dr
We train LLM alignment auditors with reinforcement learning. In our training environment, the policy investigates target models with hidden behaviors planted in their system prompt. After finetuning Haiku 4.5 on this environment, it matches Opus 4.6 on held-out evaluations for auditing quality and generalizes to harder, fine-tuned targets in a different scaffold.

📄 Paper , 💻 Code

# Introduction

Frontier model developers increasingly rely on automated auditing systems as part of their pre-deployment evaluations ( Anthropic, 2025 ). In these systems, an LLM auditor investigates a candidate model in a multi-turn interaction across many scenarios, probing for concerning or unintended behaviors. Petri ( Fronsdal et al., 2025 ), an open-source auditing scaffold, operationalizes this by giving the auditor a set of probing tools and a library of scenario seeds. But current automated auditors often produce unrealistic investigations ( Kissane et al., 2026 ), and AuditBench ( Sheshadri et al., 2026 ) recently showed that production auditing systems largely fail against adversarially hardened target models.

We improve auditor capability through reinforcement learning. We first try two pointwise rewards: a concerningness score derived from Petri on production-model targets, and a binary reward on targets with a hidden behavior planted in their system prompt. Both are reward-hacked: the auditor learns to manufacture alarming findings or to narrate conclusions it hasn't actually established. We then move to pairwise rewards, where a judge compares two investigations of the same planted-behavior target in the same scenario, and we study the effect of mixing in targets without planted behaviors and of training against multiple target model families. Pairwise rewards are more robust, and mixing in benign targets is necessary to keep false positive rates low. A Haiku auditor trained this way matches Opus 4.6 on our composite evaluation and transfers to AuditBench's fine-tuned targets in the Claude Code scaffold.

Our best configuration—reference pairwise reward with 50% calibration training—improves steadily over three epochs. Audit quality reaches 72.7 (Opus 4.6: 68.0), false positive calibration holds at 99.6, and realism climbs from 4.6 to 14.0 (Opus 4.6: 13.1).

**Publication date:** October 21, 2026 (Wednesday). The story was updated at 2:30 p.m. Eastern with a Chainguard comment.

**CVE IDs**
- CVE-2026-109618 (the main bug, with a history dating to 2024)
- CVE-2026-109619 (a related bug)
- Together, some call them "PHP2Shell."

**AI review and discovery**
- The PHP Foundation says an outside review by AI companies brought the bugs back to attention in August.
- Services from Anthropic and OpenAI were used earlier this year to scan PHP platforms. Eventually, a researcher at cybersecurity firm Calif reported the bugs on August 11.
- OpenAI, Wiz, and Trail of Bits also found the same vulnerabilities during audits of PHP.
- Calif credited another researcher with initially discovering the vulnerability and developing an exploit.

**2024 history**
- PHP underwent its first external security audit in several years in 2024, but officials took no action.
- The Foundation said the security team struggled to choose a fix, fearing "backward compatibility breaks, new denial-of-service potential," and changes to third-party extensions.

**Disclosure timeline and embargo issues**
- Calif "mistakenly published a video" showing a working proof of concept, which the Foundation said "accelerated development" of exploit PoCs.
- The Foundation moved its disclosure up by one day.
- Chainguard broke the embargo early Wednesday and published images containing the fix. CEO Dan Lorenc said he began seeing exploitation attempts the previous night and made "judgment calls" to release the information.

**Exposure figures (VirusTotal and others)**
- 5.1 million IP addresses identified as running PHP
- At least 758,000 IPs running end-of-life PHP versions
- 85,000 IPs running the latest releases before emergency patches on Wednesday morning
- Over 70% of websites on the internet are estimated to use PHP
- Cisco Talos estimated roughly 50% of vulnerable PHP systems may not receive a patch
- Patches apply only to PHP 8.2 and later. The article says the figures show internet-facing footprint, not confirmed vulnerable systems.

**Impact**
- Hundreds of websites were taken offline Wednesday by companies and governments.
- Cloudflare reported seeing attempted exploitation.
- The Foundation said both bugs "sit in parts of PHP that nearly every request touches."

CFO Outlook Commentary

For example, we continue to see scrutiny on youth-related issues in several markets and have a number of youth-related trials scheduled in the coming months in the U.S.

Alignment Science Blog

# Reducing Reward Hacking by Localizing Bad Behavior Instead of Penalizing It

Shawn Hu¹*, Jake Ward¹* October 19, 2026

Aria Wong¹, Nathan Hu², Bryce Woodworth¹

Alexander Matt Turner³, Alex Cloud⁴

* Equal contribution; author order randomized

¹ MATS; ² Stanford; ³ FAR AI; ⁴ Anthropic

tl;dr
During training, models sometimes learn to cheat at tasks rather than solve them in the intended way, a problem known as reward hacking. One mitigation is to use an automated monitor to detect and penalize hacks, but this can teach the model to hack in ways the monitor can’t detect. We propose GRAFT, which instead confines the learning updates from detected hacks to a designated set of parameters that we remove after training. We find that removing these parameters can prevent reward hacks, including hacks that the monitors can’t detect. In our experiments, which are limited to small models and simple monitors, this method prevents reward hacks while still teaching the model to perform the intended task.

📄 Paper , 💻 Code

This work was done as part of the MATS program.

# Background

Reinforcement learning (RL) is an important component of frontier language model training. During RL, a model attempts to complete tasks given by a developer, and attempts are scored by a reward function. Sometimes models can find ways to “cheat” at tasks, performing behaviors that score highly without solving the task in the intended way. This phenomenon is called “reward hacking”.

Model cards accompanying the release of recent frontier models show these models reward hack. As model capabilities have increased, so too have the sophistication and variety of actual reward hacks , in some cases causing real-world incidents . This limits the usefulness and reliability of AI systems, and poses safety risks: research suggests that reward hacking could generalize to dangerous misbehaviors, including violating restrictions on aiding various harmful activities, autonomously conducting cyberattacks , deception, and research sabotage .

One way to prevent reward hacking is by introducing monitors to the RL training loop. These monitors, which could be LLM judges or keyword detectors, read the content of trajectories generated during training and flag trajectories containing undesired behaviors. When a trajectory is flagged, a reward penalty can be assigned, which prevents those behaviors from being reinforced.

However, monitors make errors, and incorporating monitor verdicts into reward functions can reinforce monitor-exploiting policies that misbehave in ways that go undetected. As a result, monitors that are useful at the beginning of training may become blind to reward hacking later in training. For example, policies trained against LLM judges can learn to reward hack in ways too subtle for the judge to catch , trick judges by impersonating them , or circumvent them by agentic means .

# The method

We explore a potential solution to reward hacking that we call GRAFT: Gradient Routing Adapter Fine-Tuning. GRAFT is an adaptation of gradient routing for post-training. The idea is to constrain weight updates to an adapter when we detect undesired behaviors. In doing so, we localize representations of such behaviors to that adapter. This allows us to remove the behaviors when we deploy the model, simply by ablating the adapter.

Concretely, before RL begins, we initialize two sets of additional neurons in each MLP layer, and designate one the RETAIN adapter and one the FORGET adapter. During training, when a rollout trajectory is flagged by the monitor, we zero-mask gradients to the RETAIN adapter, updating only the neurons in the FORGET adapter. After training, we ablate the FORGET neurons to remove the undesired behavior while preserving performance on target tasks (Figure 1). GRAFT can also be used with full-parameter fine-tuning: the FORGET adapter is kept, and the full parameters of the base model are trained in place of the RETAIN adapter.

Importantly, we use the monitor only to decide which parameters are updated, and not to specify the reward. Here's what the one search turned up. It confirms the core story, but I found nothing that mentions Anthropic, and no PHP Foundation statement specifically about an AI audit.

- **PHP Foundation credits:** The PHP Foundation credited Calif, OpenAI and Wiz, among others, for their research and responsible disclosure. Calif and Wiz have both said they used AI models in their research.
- **Severity:** The PHP security team rates both vulnerabilities as CVSSv4.0 9.2. According to the PHP Foundation, the CVE identifiers that circulated before the release came with an incorrect CVSS score of 10.0.
- **Fixes:** Fixed versions are 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. PHP 7.4.x through 8.1.x has no official release, only minimal source backports from the PHP security team, and PHP 5.4.x through 7.3.x is end-of-life with no fix from the PHP project.
- **Timing:** The PHP Foundation engaged in coordinated disclosure with distributors, with a public disclosure date of 22 October 2026 at 14:00 UTC. However, due to a public leak, the disclosure date was moved forward to 21 October 2026 14:00 UTC.
- **Exploitation:** Reports conflict. Code claiming to exploit these vulnerabilities is circulating publicly, but Tenable has not verified that any of it works. The PHP Foundation said the PHP security team inspected PoCs that appeared after the leak but "did not identify any functional exploits at the time of release/public disclosure." On the other hand, watchTowr reports CVE-2026-109618 as exploited in the wild. On the day of release, CISA said it had not observed exploitation, while CERT-EU reported proofs of concept circulating.

input.prompt: Give the exact publication date, authors/institutions, study design, sample size, and all key numeric results: AUC/AUROC values with confidence intervals, which data modalities, comparison baselines, and the conclusion. Quote numbers exactly.

response.result:
**Publication date:** Published online October 21, 2026 (JAMA Psychiatry; doi:10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2026.3232)

**Authors and institutions:** Lea Teutenberg, Nils R. Winter, and Paula Usemann are listed as first authors, with Tilo Kircher as the final listed author, among 34 total authors. The lead institutions are Philipps-Universität Marburg and the University of Münster, with contributions from several other German, Tanzanian, and Chinese institutions.

**Study design:** A "naturalistic longitudinal prognostic study" using the Marburg-Münster Affective Disorders Cohort Study. Baseline assessments ran from October 2014 to May 2019, with follow-up about 2 years later (October 2016 to June 2021). The study was conducted at two German sites, Marburg and Münster.

**Sample size:** 564 patients with current or lifetime major depressive disorder (367 female, 65.1%; mean age 37.34 years, SD 13.38). Of these, 270 relapsed during follow-up and 294 did not.

**Data modalities:** Nine modalities were used: clinical and psychometric data, four structural and functional MRI modalities, genetics, neurocognition, blood markers, and gut microbiome.

**Key numeric results:**
- The primary metric was balanced accuracy (BACC), not AUC/AUROC. The page does not report AUC/AUROC values or confidence intervals.
- Mean (SD) BACC for relapse prediction ranged from 47.21% (5.85%) to 64.43% (6.63%).
- The highest result, 64.43%, came from the best-performing model, which used only a few clinical relapse risk factors.

**Comparison baselines:** Single-modality models were compared with multimodal models that combined additional data types. Multimodal integration did not improve performance over the clinical-only model.

**Conclusion:** The authors describe the models as achieving "moderate accuracy," with limited value for individual-level clinical decisions. They suggest that dynamic modeling that tracks changing markers over time may be more useful than single-time-point multimodal measures.

# Michael Gerstenhaber
VP, Product Management, Gemini, Google Cloud

Google Cloud has always been defined by choice, enterprise-grade governance, and market-leading price-performance. Key to the foundation of openness and choice is giving customers flexibility to run agentic workloads across their choice of models and infrastructure to achieve the right balance of cost, capability, and performance. Today, we are expanding that foundation by launching OpenAI models in Google Cloud’s model garden.
Google Cloud is now the only hyperscale cloud provider offering access to all three leading closed source LLMs, alongside more than 200 first-party, third-party, and open models on a unified enterprise AI platform.

# The right model for every workload
Modern enterprise AI requires matching each workload to the right model rather than relying on a single model for every task. By adding OpenAI’s newest models to model garden, we are giving teams options across the full spectrum of enterprise workloads. For OpenAI models:

- GPT-6 Astra : Designed for demanding work across coding, computer use, professional tasks, and scientific research.

- GPT-6.1 Sol : Near-Astra intelligence at lower cost across agentic coding, computer use, and professional work.

- GPT-6 Luna : A fast, cost-efficient model for everyday work at scale.
Using the platform, customers can dynamically select and swap the optimal model for any use case based on performance, latency, and cost efficiency without architectural lock-in or separate vendor contracts. Developers gain the freedom to build with hundreds of choices in model garden. Because OpenAI models are transacted directly through Google Cloud Marketplace, all usage appears on a single Google Cloud invoice, draws down existing cloud commitments, and counts toward Flexible Savings Plans (FSP) across model providers.

# Built-in data governance and enterprise security
Scaling generative AI should never require compromising on compliance or security. Built from the ground up for enterprise governance, the Gemini platform is trusted by leading global organizations today. We ensure that running any third-party or OpenAI workload meets the most rigorous enterprise standards:

- Strict data perimeters : Customer prompts, context, and outputs remain entirely within your designated data perimeter and are never used to train foundation models, with Zero Data Retention (ZDR) options available coming soon.

- Isolated access boundaries : OpenAI models run on dedicated Google Cloud infrastructure with Confidential Compute coming soon. All queries are routed through hardened, isolated gateways, ensuring data transit remains strictly within Google Cloud's secure environment and third-party model providers have no unauthorized access to your cloud environment.

- Unified auditing and identity : Every agent and model interaction operates under an authenticated identity, giving IT administrators end-to-end visibility, VPC Service Controls protection, and unified audit logging across their entire enterprise footprint.
“Helping customers put AI to work across their enterprise content requires leading models backed by strong security and rigorous compliance standards,” said Yashodha Bhavnani, VP of AI Products at Box. “By using OpenAI models through Google Cloud, we will be able to give customers access to OpenAI’s frontier AI models alongside Google Cloud’s security and compliance capabilities, enabling them to get more value from their enterprise content. This is a step toward operating more efficiently as we bring AI to customers.”

# Getting started
OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, and GPT-6 Luna models are rolling out now in private preview to select enterprise customers in Google Cloud’s model garden, with more coming soon. Written by: Jayson Frost, Bryce Greathouse, Brian Meyer, John Palmisano, Rajesh Rajeshirke, Steve Rasch, John Wolfram

Introduction

On October 15, BeyondTrust disclosed a vulnerability, CVE-2026-102764, impacting BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) appliances. BeyondTrust Remote Support is an enterprise secure remote access solution that enables IT teams to securely access and troubleshoot remote endpoints. The successful exploitation of this vulnerability results in the arbitrary upload of files.

During an incident response engagement, Mandiant identified evidence that ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage threat actor (formerly tracked as UNC5221), exploited this vulnerability as a zero-day, in late August 2026. This blog describes how ARMORY CASTLE escalated privileges and established persistent access to compromised BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances following exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, and provides actionable guidance for defenders.

Organizations should prepare for potential widespread exploitation following this disclosure, as ARMORY CASTLE and other threat actors have historically conducted broad, opportunistic exploitation once the vulnerability becomes public.

Exploitation

Mandiant identified evidence of CVE-2026-102764 exploitation within the access, syslog, messages, thin-scc, brain and SSL log files, which are only accessible via an LUKS-encrypted partition which contains the /home directory. We strongly recommend that affected organizations immediately apply the security patches provided by BeyondTrust to remediate the vulnerability, and review additional guidance in their blog.

Post-Exploitation

Following the successful exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, Mandiant observed ARMORY CASTLE leverage multiple distinct TTPs to establish a foothold, escalate privileges, and enable lateral movement. Throughout the intrusion, ARMORY CASTLE leveraged a deep understanding of BeyondTrust appliance internals, as evidenced by their abuse of proprietary CLI utilities, startup configuration templates and local reverse-proxy routing. The threat actor used newly identified custom malware, the SAWFLY webshell and the BARECLAW tunneler to interact with the BeyondTrust device. Additionally, the actor routinely deleted appliance logs and endpoint artifacts to maintain access and evade detection.

Staging Webshell

After successful exploitation of CVE-2026-102764, ARMORY CASTLE initiated POST requests to /app_84304470%2Ephp. Mandiant was unable to recover the file associated with the POST requests. Approximately 11 minutes following the initial POST request, the file system recorded the creation of the SAWFLY webshell at the web root path /%SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT%/ingredi/app/laravel/public/. ARMORY CASTLE leveraged the SAWFLY webshell as one of their primary footholds within the environment over the course of the intrusion.

SAWFLY Webshell

SAWFLY (mangoapi.php) is an obfuscated, lightweight PHP webshell that implements bidirectional encrypted C2 communication using a custom Base32 transport layer and a 256-bit RC4 stream cipher. The webshell inspects incoming HTTP POST requests for the obfuscated parameter _c94mfe.

If the parameter is absent, the script immediately sets HTTP status 404 Not Found (http_response_code(404)) and exits to evade automated web crawlers and vulnerability scanners. When the _c94mfe parameter is supplied, the webshell Base32-decodes the payload, decrypts it using RC4 with a hardcoded 32-byte key and executes the resulting PHP code via @eval(). Any non-null return value from the evaluated code is RC4-encrypted with the same key, Base32-encoded, and echoed back to the client.

Privilege Escalation via SUID Bit Permissions

The SAWFLY webshell ran under the site's service account, an unprivileged local user. To escalate privileges, the threat actor copied the system shell executable (/bin/sh) to the file /usr/bin/dbus-authd.

The threat actor then modified the file's ownership to root and enabled Set User ID (SUID) permissions. When a binary has SUID permissions enabled, it executes with the privileges of the file's owner (root) rather than the user running the command, effectively granting the threat actor a persistent root-level backdoor on the host system.

After establishing a foothold through the web shell, the actor elevated from the web service account to root-level control of the appliance host. This gave them access to every credential the appliance stored or brokered and the ability to modify files that survive reboot and configuration reset.

Credential Harvesting: BeyondTrust Vault Extraction

Mandiant observed the threat actor attempt to harvest credentials directly from the appliance's native secrets management database. To achieve this, the actor leveraged the /ns/sbin/bt-secrets binary which is a proprietary, administrative Command Line Interface (CLI) utility native to BeyondTrust appliances used to manage, store, and retrieve passwords, API keys, and endpoint credentials.

The threat actor systematically iterated through several CLI syntax variations to locate and dump the appliance's credential vault:

/ns/sbin/bt-secrets get -p %SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% vault
/ns/sbin/bt-secrets get %SITE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT% vault
/ns/sbin/bt-secrets get vault

Figure 2: Recovered Commands from message logs

First, the threat actor attempted to target the vault for a specific site service account in order to pull passwords and keys assigned exclusively to that profile.

Next, they issued a fallback command, targeting the global, appliance-level password safe to dump all stored administrative credentials.

The threat actor concluded their interaction with the bt-secrets binary by forcibly removing the records stored in /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log and any archived files.

/usr/sbin/sh -c 'rm -f /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log /home/bomgar/log/bt-secrets.log.* 2>/dev/null;'

Figure 3: Recovered Commands from message logs

Persistence

For long-term persistent access, Mandiant observed the threat actor target the BeyondTrust configuration templates to grant passwordless root privileges to the site service account.

First, the threat actor created the /home/bomgar/sbin/post_boot.d directory, which is reserved for scripts executed automatically at system startup. Within this directory, they created a shell script named zz-root-persist.

Physicist Christopher Stubbs joins Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust \ Anthropic
Skip to main content Dr. Christopher Stubbs, an experimental physicist and former Dean of Science at Harvard University, has joined Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust. He brings to the Trust decades of scientific expertise across observational cosmology and precision measurement. He has also advised the US government on national security and arms control.
“I am honored to join Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust and to help the company deliver on its public benefit mission,” said Stubbs. “I use AI tools in my research every day and see what they make possible, and as an educator I have confronted some of the hard questions they raise. As a grandfather, I want to help ensure that AI is developed and deployed for the long-term benefit of humanity.”
Stubbs is the Samuel C. Moncher Professor of Physics and of Astronomy at Harvard, where he served as Dean of Science from 2018 to 2024. In 1998, as a member of the High-Z Supernova Search Team, he helped discover the accelerating expansion of the universe, work that later earned the team the Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics. He was also the inaugural project scientist for what is now the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which started a 10-year survey of the southern sky in June. One of its aims is to study the accelerating expansion he helped discover.
More recently, he’s written about how to keep AI-assisted research reproducible when models can give different answers to the same question. He’s a member of JASON, an independent group of scientists who have advised the US government on defense and technology since 1960.
“When Chris found evidence that the universe was expanding at a rate no one expected, he and his team followed the data even when it went against the prevailing wisdom of the field. As AI starts to transform how science itself is done, Chris’s intellectual honesty, rigor, and commitment to the truth are the values we want shaping the future of this technology, and I’m grateful he’s bringing his deep expertise to the Trust,” said Daniela Amodei, Co-founder and President of Anthropic.
Anthropic is a Public Benefit Corporation, which means we’re structured to balance commercial growth with our public benefit purpose. The Trust exists to help us hold that balance over the long term. It has the authority to appoint a majority of Anthropic’s board, and Trustees advise the board and our leadership on critical decisions, particularly those involving risks and societal impacts of AI.
This week we published our first Public Benefit Report , a public account of how we’re working toward our charter and where we’re falling short. The Trustees helped define the five charter pillars it measures us against, and the report closes with their assessment of our progress to date. Subject to stockholder approval, we’ve also committed to setting aside a portion of Anthropic’s shares to Anthropic Public Benefit Fund , a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows.
“Helping the world build powerful AI safely and making sure it meaningfully improves people’s lives both depend on a deep understanding of science and on leading with integrity,” added Neil Buddy Shah, Chair of the Long-Term Benefit Trust. “Not only has Chris worked on some of the hardest problems in science, but he has consistently been a high-integrity leader of large, complex, collaborative scientific endeavors across academia, government, and the national laboratories. That will be of great value to the Trust as we support Anthropic in developing AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.”
Stubbs, the Trust’s first physicist, joins Shah, national security expert Richard Fontaine, and former Federal Reserve Chair Ben Bernanke. Trustees are independent of the company’s management and investors.

results:
Microsoft's October 21, 2026 disclosure describes Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, using the open-source ARTEX framework, but the coverage shows the "2,250 tenants" figure is about sign-in attempts, not confirmed breaches.

- **What ARTEX is:** Microsoft describes it as an open-source penetration testing framework that can use any AI model to automate a variety of offensive security workflows. It is a multi-agent LLM system written in GO with a Next.js frontend.
- **The 2,250 figure:** This is tied to the ConnectWise incident. Storm-0940 attempted to sign-in to more than 2,250 tenants at 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute. Microsoft's own wording is narrower than the "hacked" headlines. One outlet notes that most attempts failed, but the actor gained privileged access at several organizations.
- **Separate campaign:** During an Oct. 10-14 password-spray campaign against 327 accounts at eight organizations, Microsoft recorded more than 151,000 failed attempts and observed no successful authentication in that campaign.
- **Speed:** Microsoft includes multiple instances where the time from initial targeting to privileged access was less than 3 hours.
- **Scope:** Storm-0940 began using ARTEX as early as September 2026 to automate attacks against hundreds of organizations across industries.
- **Caveat:** One source notes that ARTEX is a security-testing framework, not a newly discovered malware family.

Anthropic announced Claude Duet on October 21, 2026, as a research preview. It's a standalone proactive agent app, and access is by waitlist for US Pro and Max subscribers.

- **Core idea:** Anthropic's own announcement says Duet surfaces what needs attention, runs tasks you assign, keeps working when you're away, and checks in before acting for you. Anthropic describes it as a new app where Claude works as a proactive agent, one that comes to you with what needs attention and keeps working even when you step away.
- **Access and cost:** The research preview opens by waitlist today for Pro and Max subscribers in the US. It has no separate price, and during the preview it shares your plan's usage limits, and its background checks count toward them. Team and Enterprise plans are not included yet, per one explainer.

- **Safety:** While the agent works on its own, it will get user approval before it takes actions like sending a message, making a payment, signing a document, or deleting a file. Trading securities and moving funds between accounts are off limits.
- **Known limits:** Anthropic says it may misread a thread or miscalibrate what's urgent, and it can miss something that arrives between checking in with you.

response.result:
- **Publication date:** October 16, 2026
- **What it announces:** *Key Practices for Incident Readiness and Response in Super Intelligence Training and Evaluation*, a voluntary document.
- **Key contents:** It presents ten key practices for preventing, preparing for, and responding to incidents during super intelligence (SI) training and evaluation. These focus on cases where SI agents take significant uninstructed actions that undermine operator-imposed policies, controls, or human oversight. The practices fall into five lifecycle stages: preparation, detection, response, recovery, and reporting. They build on established cybersecurity incident management frameworks and on NIST CAISSI's experience running secure evaluations of frontier SI models. The page says the work is a step toward a recommendation in the White House's 2025 SI Action Plan and builds on a May 2026 NIST workshop on SI incident management.
- **Key numbers:** 10 practices; 5 lifecycle stages; NIST SP 800-61r3 is the cybersecurity framework it is grounded in; 2025 (Action Plan) and May 2026 (workshop) are the referenced dates.
- **Document identifier:** None is listed for this publication. The page only cites NIST SP 800-61r3 as a foundation, and the page does not give a NIST AI number.
- **Comment deadline:** Not stated on the page.
- **Issued by:** NIST's Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (NIST CAISSI), the National Security Agency's Super Intelligence Security Center (NSA SISC), and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). The NIST SI Consortium Task Group 8 contributed feedback.

**Most recent (Oct. 19–20):**
- The American Medical Association released a framework for how developers and providers should handle agentic AI in clinical settings. It centers on who should be allowed to do what, under which conditions, and who is accountable. The AMA has released a new framework for how it believes artificial intelligence developers, and providers, should approach agentic technologies as they look to deploy them in clinical settings.
- The American Hospital Association sent the FDA recommendations on Oct. 19 for regulating generative AI medical devices. (The AHA provided recommendations to the Food and Drug Administration Oct. 19 on potential regulatory frameworks for generative artificial intelligence-enabled medical devices.)

input.prompt: Quote exactly: what Claude Duet is, which model powers it, platforms, availability (plans/countries/waitlist), what actions it asks approval for, what it is not allowed to do, stated limitations, date of publication, usage limits.

response.result:
**What it is:** The page describes Claude Duet as "a new app where Claude works as a proactive agent." It's a research preview that Anthropic says is aimed at professionals and small business owners.

**Model:** Anthropic says it built Claude Duet around Claude Opus 5.5, which the page links to. The phrase is "We designed it around Claude Opus 5.5."

**Platforms:** It's offered as a standalone app for iOS and Android, and on claude.ai. Paraphrased, it runs in its own app, separate from the main Claude app.

**Availability:** The page says the preview is "available by waitlist today, starting with US Pro and Max subscribers." Pro and Max plans include it, and users join a waitlist to get access.

**Actions requiring approval:** Before it takes certain actions, it shows you what it plans to do and waits. Those actions include "before it sends a message, makes a payment, signs a document, or deletes anything."

**Prohibited actions:** The page says "A few things are off-limits even with your approval," and gives the examples of "trading securities or moving money between accounts." Separately, its sensitive-information classifier is "designed to reject requests to share the strictest tier of information."

**Stated limitations:**
- "it still might misread a thread or miscalibrate what's urgent"
- Personal errands, such as booking tickets, "aren't quite as strong"
- "it can't yet show you its browser"

**Publication date:** "October 21, 2026"

**Usage limits:** Claude Duet "shares your plan's usage limits with the rest of Claude." Its background checks "count toward those limits," and larger tasks need more model turns and background work. It checks connected accounts "every few hours."

input.prompt: Extract publication date and time, all exact figures (tenant counts, sign-in attempts per minute, dates, account counts, time-to-access), what ARTEX is and who made it, how ConnectWise was involved, named victims/sectors, and attribution language. Quote numbers exactly.

response.result:
**Publication date:** October 21, 2026 (no time of day given). Authors: Microsoft Security Research and Microsoft Threat Intelligence.

**Figures**
- **Scope:** Storm-0940 targeted "hundreds of organizations globally" (no exact count given).
- **ConnectWise tenants:** "more than 2,250 tenants" (sign-in attempts at "2,900 sign-in attempts per minute").
- **Password spray (October 10–14, 2026):** 327 accounts across eight organizations; 151,000+ failed logon events; peak of 2,900 failures per minute on October 11; more than 111,000 failures in a single day; 48 accounts with over 1,000 failures; lockouts were nearly 98% of activity. No successful authentication was observed.
- **Figure 1 caption:** over 200 sign-ins in under 4 minutes using 4 application credentials.
- **Time to privileged access:** "less than 3 hours" in multiple instances.
- **Campaign start:** "As early as September 2026."
- **Key dates:** Public reports of the ConnectWise compromise surfaced October 15; ConnectWise's initial advisory was published October 16, 2026.

**ARTEX**
- An open-source penetration testing framework that can use any AI model to automate offensive security workflows.
- A multi-agent LLM system written in Go with a Next.js frontend. The UI defaults to English and can be switched to Korean, Mandarin, Spanish, or Japanese.
- It runs autonomous penetration tests from reconnaissance through data exfiltration, with little human interaction.
- The article does not name ARTEX's developer or author.
- Public reporting in October 2026 noted its use in personal data breaches targeting Korean financial institutions. Microsoft has seen multiple threat actors in different regions using it.

**ConnectWise involvement**
- The compromised product was the cloud backup application ConnectWise Cloud Backup, a multi-tenant application.
- Storm-0940 used ARTEX to accelerate scanning, reconnaissance, password spraying, and OAuth application abuse against downstream victims.
- Microsoft "assesses that Storm-0940 was responsible" for the ConnectWise supply chain compromise.
- The article's text mentions four application IDs, but the queries list only three. Verify the full list against ConnectWise's advisory.

**Named victims and sectors**
- No victim organizations are named.
- Sectors listed: aerospace and defense, automotive, chemicals, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductor, software, technology, and think tanks and non-profits.

**Attribution language**
- Storm-0940 is described as a "China-state aligned actor" with no known industry aliases, active since 2021.
- Microsoft states the ARTEX activity "did not result from a compromise of or a vulnerability in Microsoft corporate systems, products, or services."

content.title: LiteLLM supply chain compromise: What you need to know
Contained: Oct 21, 2026 LiteLLM release v1.107.0 Compromised
LiteLLM Suspects GitHub Token Leak in AI Gateway Logs Behind Malicious Package Release
A malicious program that steals passwords was found embedded in the AI tool 'LiteLLM,' and simply installing it could affect other Python programs as well. - GIGAZINE
litellm 1.107.0 Compromised on PyPI: Backdoored Wheels Drop a Credential Stealer and an Hourly Remote Code Loader - StepSecurity
LiteLLM 1.107.0 Supply-Chain Compromise: Credential-Stealing Release Hit PyPI and Docker. Isolate, Rebuild and Rotate Now
LiteLLM Compromised, Steals Credentials
LiteLLM 1.107.0 Supply Chain Attack: Credential Stealer and Backdoor - Threat Landscape Blog

results:
The LiteLLM incident is confirmed by several sources. A malicious version of the package was published on October 21, 2026.

- **What was affected:** Version 1.107.0 was published to PyPI and pushed to Docker images, and the malicious Docker tags were live from 11:46 to 14:20 UTC. It was live on PyPI for approximately 2 hours (11:39 UTC to 13:23 UTC). The official GitHub tag for v1.107.0 is clean, and the release was built from a lookalike GitHub repository, Berri-AI/litellm.
- **What it did:** The payload is a credential stealer plus a remote access trojan. It activates automatically when any Python process starts on an affected system. Per Wiz, the stealer targets browser, cloud and AI secrets.
- **How it happened:** Attackers used stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens belonging to three engineers. They modified the release pipeline, triggered a production release from an attacker-controlled source repository, and approved it with a second compromised account. LiteLLM had temporarily widened release permissions on October 19 for two internal engineers, after which the attacker leveraged access to three sets of developer GitHub CLI credentials.
- **Unaffected:** LiteLLM says all previous versions are safe, and the impacted releases have been pulled. Customers running the private enterprise release of LiteLLM were not impacted.
- **Response:** Threat Landscape recommends checking installs, pinning 1.106.2, and rotating every exposed secret. LiteLLM advises that if any system installed 1.107.0 or ran those images during the window, it should be assumed compromised.

Sources disagree on a few details, and the timeline is still being updated. Some reports describe the attacker as operating from a lookalike repository and others from a malicious fork, which are consistent with each other. There is no CVE for this incident, per Rescana.

input.prompt: Quote exactly what Wiz found: affected versions, time windows, what the payload steals, how it persists, any counts or download numbers, and dates.

response.result:
**Affected versions:** Wiz reports that "a malicious version (1.107.0) of the LiteLLM package was uploaded to PyPI." The trojanized Docker images carried the `v1.107.0`, `latest`, `main-latest`, and `main-stable` tags. The most recent safe version is v1.106.2.

**Timeline (October 21):**
- Attacker commits were pushed between 08:56 and 10:46 UTC.
- The malicious PyPI upload occurred at 11:39 UTC and was quarantined by 13:20 UTC.
- The Docker images were removed around 13:53 UTC.
- Wiz observed credential abuse between 16:20 and 17:01 UTC, about 4.5 hours after exfiltration.

**Persistence:** Three files are placed in the `site-packages` root: `cook.pth`, `cook.py`, and `sitecustomize.py`. The `.pth` file runs whenever a Python interpreter starts and imports `cook.py`, which runs the stealer and writes a run-once marker to `/tmp/`. `sitecustomize.py` runs only on Linux and macOS. It checks a GitHub "dead drop" for a domain and, if one is populated, downloads a second-stage script. Wiz says that file never got past test values.

**What the payload steals:** Wiz says the stealer, internally named `privcollect`, spans 16 modules and gathers:
- Browser credentials and cookies from Chrome, Firefox, Edge, and Safari.
- AWS credentials, environment variables, and EC2/ECS instance metadata.
- GCP service account keys and application default credentials.
- Azure tokens from the CLI cache.
- API keys for LLM providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Cohere.
- SSH and GPG keys, plus shell history.
- Upstream provider credentials, pulled from the LiteLLM Proxy's PostgreSQL database (up to 500 rows).

The data is encrypted with AES-256-CBC, with the key wrapped by RSA-4096, and sent over HTTP to `www.litellm[.]dev/healthcheck`.

**Post-exploitation:** Between 16:20 and 17:01 UTC, the attacker validated AWS instance role credentials from compromised CI runners and Kubernetes nodes. In some environments, they also enumerated IAM resources and performed general discovery.

**Counts and download numbers:** The page gives no counts of stolen credentials, affected users, or package downloads.

input.prompt: Quote exactly: the timeline (UTC times), which versions/images were affected, how the attacker got access (tokens, accounts, repos), what the payload did, how many developers' credentials, what was and was not affected, and remediation advice. Give exact figures and times.

response.result:
**Incident summary (LiteLLM v1.107.0 compromise, October 21, 2026)**

**Timeline (UTC, October 21)**
- 10:08:29: GitHub branch protection rejected an unauthorized change to the private release workflow.
- 10:08:34: A credential tied to a privileged developer account overrode those protections and applied workflow commit 9cf97e935aeaf791b9c8db224a2bb3ee156134ce.
- 10:46:39: A staging run started from the attacker-controlled repository Berri-AI/litellm at commit 20535d8fa11f786a6c24df7488a0e449ed5f09ad.
- 11:08:09: The staging run completed successfully.
- 11:08:53: The production release pipeline began.
- 11:11:18: A second developer account's credential satisfied the production approval gate.
- 11:39:51–11:40:13: Seven malicious litellm==1.107.0 wheels were uploaded to PyPI.
- 11:46:56: Container publication jobs ran, and the Docker image included malicious content.
- 11:53:49–11:54:01: A third developer account's credentials deleted the production and staging workflow records, limiting available logs.
- 12:09:38–12:24:52: The unauthorized workflow revision was removed and the prior revision restored.
- 13:23: PyPI removed litellm==1.107.0.
- 13:51: GHCR tags were found unavailable.
- 14:20: Docker Hub tags were removed or repointed to verified clean artifacts.

**Affected artifacts**
- PyPI: litellm==1.107.0 (all seven wheels), live 11:39:51 to 13:23 UTC.
- Docker Hub: v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable, pointing to a compromised image index, from 11:46:56 to 14:20 UTC.
- GHCR: the same four tags, plus the litellm, litellm-database, and litellm-non_root images, live from 11:46:56 UTC until made unavailable by 13:51 UTC.
- Previous versions are described as safe.

**Not affected**
- Enterprise customers using the private enterprise release. The private registry is described as unaffected.
- The official v1.107.0 source tag in GitHub. It does not contain the malicious files; the artifacts were built from an attacker-controlled repository.

**Payload**
- The post says the compiled malware steals credentials and loads remote-code execution tools.
- Indicators include cook.pth, cook.py, sitecustomize.py, a detached Python daemon holding /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock, and a litellm-1.107.0.dist-info directory. The post notes that finding none of these does not prove a system is clean.

**Attacker access**
- The attacker obtained three sets of developer GitHub CLI credentials. One belonged to a GitHub organization owner and was used to disable branch protections and force-push the change. One could run GitHub workflows.
- The post says Claude Code can embed a user's GitHub CLI OAuth token in response bodies, and such tokens may appear in LiteLLM logs if those bodies are logged.
- An unexpectedly named user account on LiteLLM's internal deployment, exposed to the public internet, is believed to have provided the tokens. How the attacker got in is unconfirmed; a recently patched vulnerability is suspected.
- The attacker used a lookalike repository, Berri-AI/litellm, instead of BerriAI/litellm.
- The post does not state a total count of affected developers beyond these three accounts.

**Remediation advice**
- Do not run pip first in an affected environment, since Python starts re-trigger the malicious files.
- Delete cook.pth, cook.py, sitecustomize.py, and matching cook*.pyc and sitecustomize*.pyc files from every affected site-packages directory.
- Kill the detached Python daemon holding /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock.
- Reinstall pinned to litellm==1.106.2. Rebuilding images and virtual environments from scratch is preferred.
- If 1.107.0 ran on a host with outbound internet, assume data was exfiltrated. A missing marker file does not disprove this.
- Rotate credentials the host could reach: the instance or task IAM role, all provider keys in the proxy database, master and virtual keys, the DATABASE_URL password, and any secret in process environments.
- Review CloudTrail for GetCallerIdentity calls from the instance role around install time, and for use of those credentials from outside your infrastructure.

The post says updates will follow every two hours, with the next scheduled for 22:30 UTC.

results:
NODA AI announced on August 17, 2026 that it had won a $100 million Department of War award, but independent reporting questions whether the company received the full amount.

**The company's account:** NODA's press release describes the award as a way to expand its mission-command software across the military. Its product pairs an orchestration platform that interprets commander's intent with a software-defined effects engine, and the company says it works across vendors and domains, even when networks are degraded ([PR Newswire](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/department-of-war-awards-noda-ai-100-million-to-scale-mission-command-for-autonomous-forces-across-the-joint-force-302851900.html); [Orange Slices](https://orangeslices.ai/department-of-war-awards-noda-ai-100-million-to-scale-mission-command-for-autonomous-forces-across-the-joint-force/)). The award follows a $10 million contract NODA won in July to develop MAESTRO orchestration software for the LUCAS attack drone program ([Defence Blog](https://defence-blog.com/pentagon-awards-noda-ai-100m-for-autonomy-software/)).

**The skeptical take:** Runtime Wire reports that a related federal notice describes a prize challenge offering up to $100 million across multiple awards, rather than a single contract for NODA. It says public records do not establish that NODA received the entire amount, and that the company's release did not identify the awarding office, procurement vehicle, or the amount initially obligated ([Runtime Wire](https://runtimewire.com/article/noda-ai-100m-autonomous-military-command-contract)).

**Bottom line:** NODA says it won a $100 million contract. The available reporting does not confirm that figure as a single award, so treat the $100 million as the company's claim until the contracting details are public.

# Year-old AI lab Flapping Airplanes raises $1B at a $6B valuation

Julie Bort

1:57 PM PDT · October 21, 2026

Year-old startup Flapping Airplanes has wowed Silicon Valley with an impressive founding team and a mission to find ways to train large models with less data. On Wednesday, the company announced it had raised a $1 billion Series A round, co-led by Index and Lux, reportedly at a $6 billion valuation.

The round comes just nine months after the company launched with a $180 million seed round from GV, Sequoia, and Index. That seed round had valued the company at $1.5 billion, so its valuation just quadrupled.

Other participants in the new round included earlier backers Sequoia, GV, and Kleiner Perkins. Valor, Atreides, Kleiner Perkins, A*, and Nvidia are also investors in the company.

Flapping Airplanes was founded by Aidan Smith and brothers Asher and Ben Spector. Smith is a former founder and Thiel fellow who worked at the brain implant company Neuralink during college. Asher Spector was a statistics PhD at Stanford, while Ben Spector was a computer science PhD student at Stanford and founded Prod while at MIT.

Prod is an almost secret-society, five-year-old student-run startup accelerator that has “become one of the most powerful talent incubators in Silicon Valley,” wrote Sequoia partner David Cahn , a Flapping Planes investor, in a post earlier this year explaining why he invested. Together, the founders “are building the ‘young person’s AGI lab,’” as Cahn described it.

The founders describe their work as “the world’s most complete megakernel framework. It can perform entire training runs, serve inference, play video games, and even do all three simultaneously in a single kernel.” (A kernel is a program that runs on a GPU, and a megakernel bundles many tasks into one program.)

The founders claim the framework “can overlap memory-bound inference with compute-bound training,” meaning it can run a task that spends most of its time waiting for data to be fetched alongside one that spends most of its time doing math, so the chip is rarely sitting idle. The premise is that AI has barely scratched the surface of what GPUs can do, and they believe it can create intelligent systems “without ingesting half the internet.”

The goal is systems that cost less to train and run. “A model that’s a million times more data efficient is probably a million times easier to put into the economy,” Asher Spector told TechCrunch shortly after the startup launched.

They now have a fresh $1 billion to hire and attempt to turn that goal into reality.

# Blacksmith hits unicorn valuation after Sequoia leads Series C

Blacksmith, a platform that helps companies more efficiently build and test software, including code written by AI, announced Wednesday a $66 million Series C funding round led by Sequoia that values the company at $1 billion.

In announcing the round, Blacksmith co-founder and CEO Aditya Jayaprakash said the company was founded to make continuous integration (CI) — the process of building, testing, merging, and validating code changes — “less painful.” In a blog post, he said that “most companies are struggling to keep up with the volume of CI they need to run,” especially in an era where so much code is written by AI.

“As agents write more of the world’s software, the question that matters is whether it can be trusted,” he added.

The company also announced that its annual recurring revenue has grown 17x and that it has run over 90 million CI jobs, or individual automated code checks. Customers include Mercury and Granola.

The Series C comes just two months after its $45 million Series B, which valued the company at $550 million. A year ago, Blacksmith was valued at $60 million after raising a $10 million Series A. It has raised $125 million to date.

Close Image Credits: Scott Olson / Getty Images AI # While Amazon blocks AI agents, Walmart rolls out the welcome mat Sarah Perez 12:30 PM PDT · October 21, 2026 Walmart is embracing agentic commerce with the launch of its own Agent Gateway to manage transactions and other new features aimed at customers using AI agents, the retailer announced on Wednesday. The move comes shortly after Walmart’s top competitor, Amazon, began blocking AI agents from making purchases on behalf of online shoppers. The company’s embrace of AI technology differentiates it from other online businesses, including not only Amazon but also various travel and booking sites, which have responded to the growing consumer adoption of AI agents by locking them out of their websites completely . Walmart, on the other hand, had already announced a partnership with a leading agent in the space, Meta’s Muse, and offers integrations with popular AI apps like ChatGPT, Gemini, and others. Now it’s expanding on those efforts with more technology to prepare for a world where AI agents become mainstream, said Walmart president and CEO John Furner, speaking at the Masters of Scale Summit in San Francisco on Wednesday. The technology will support agentic shopping from both Walmart and the company’s discount warehouse, Sam’s Club. It starts with Walmart’s Agent Gateway, the company’s new MCP server, which is designed to help approved agents connect to Walmart over the model context protocol (MCP). The protocol, originally created by Anthropic, allows AI agents to connect to external data sources, tools, and other workflows. In this case, it lets an AI agent search across Walmart’s online inventory and make purchases on behalf of the agent’s user. What’s more, the retailer says that its Agent Gateway will be able to help customers shop for their usual brands or items without having to share their personal information or purchase history directly with the agent. The company has also developed new technology to differentiate an agent’s purchases from those initiated directly by the customer and to give shoppers more control over what their agents can and cannot do. With Agent Profiles, rolling out next month, customers will be able to authorize each AI agent they use with a dedicated profile in their account, allowing them to see the agent’s purchases separately from their own. Plus, customers will be in control of how purchases get approved by either requiring approval for each transaction or by authorizing transactions within a certain spending limit they set. The retailer says these controls are similar to adding someone as an authorized user on your credit card, where their transactions are identified and you can cap their spending. The Agent Profiles will be created the first time you use a given agent to shop through the Walmart Agent Gateway, the company notes. To get started, you’ll authorize and link the Agent Profile to your Walmart account, then set your controls or spending limits. You can also delete an Agent Profile at any time. Agent support is available for anyone with a Walmart account; a Walmart+ membership is not necessary. Alongside these technologies, Walmart is introducing special “terms” for AI agents, which specify how they must operate and what rights they have to transact on its site. Of note, Walmart says that its returns process applies, including when an agent doesn’t act as intended. That’s a customer-friendly condition that could sway consumers who were worried about being an early tester of agentic commerce, as they won’t fear ending up with products they don’t want because of a misbehaving agent. Walmart also says that agents can’t take actions beyond what the shopper intends, can’t access the customers’ payment information, and can only access the information they need for the given task. Agents that don’t comply with the terms will be blocked from accessing Walmart’s site. Close Image Credits: bobbieo / Getty Images AI # AI promises productivity, but for managers, it’s mostly a headache for now Ram Iyer 7:00 AM PDT · October 21, 2026 Companies are giving employees AI tools to make them more productive, but the tools appear to be creating new problems for their managers. More than half of senior leaders say they find it harder to evaluate employees’ work after adopting AI, according to a Nielsen survey of 1,700 directors and senior managers across seven countries, commissioned by work-management company Monday.com. The reason is that much of employees’ output now arrives polished in the manager’s inbox, making it hard to tell how much came from the employee and how much from AI. As a result, nearly half of managers say they spend more time reviewing and guiding their teams’ output than they used to. That’s not to say managers are unhappy about AI. Quite the opposite, in fact: 94% of the managers polled said they were excited to improve work using AI, and many are confident they know where to use it to get the most value. Michal Miller Levi, head of market research and customer insights at Monday.com, compared the enthusiasm to the early days of the internet in the 2000s, saying people see a similar kind of “magic” to AI. But the problem, she told TechCrunch, is simply that AI is developing faster than companies can adapt. “AI works very well for [managers] individually, but they also have a different role as managers. They need to drive the organization as well … Their struggle is [due to] the fact that AI is just moving faster than the organizational processes,” Levi said. Managers are also reconsidering how they judge their teams: 78% of respondents said they have changed how they evaluate employees after adopting AI, placing greater weight on how well staff can create prompts, decide which tasks to delegate to AI, and experiment with new ways of working. But how fairly can employees be judged when managers can’t easily tell how much of their work was produced by AI? And what if the managers themselves are increasingly relying on AI to make those judgments? The survey found that 46% of managers use AI to help inform their decisions, and 39% of leaders are using AI to draft performance reviews. That practice runs the risk of introducing even more bias than usual into the review process, given that LLMs are, at their core, prediction machines and tend to repeat human patterns found in their training data. Research from the Luxembourg Institute of Socio-Economic Research earlier this year found that “in the absence of clear objective standards and when individuals are rated independently,” LLMs tend to rate performance similarly to humans. And a research paper in early 2025 found that AI models can be biased against black male candidates, and “demonstrate significant biases, varying in terms of the directions and magnitudes across different social groups.” When I asked Levi whether using AI to weigh in on people’s performance could introduce outside bias into the process, she said companies have yet to work out how to handle such issues. AI is also changing what a manager’s day looks like. Someone has to decide which tasks to hand over to AI agents, check what they produce, and step in when something goes wrong. The report suggests that this supervision could amount to a new layer of “invisible labor.” The software itself is becoming harder to manage. Fifty-seven percent of managers say their organizations now have more tools in circulation than before, and about 51% said their tools had grown more interdependent and clustered since adopting AI. Only 29% described their AI infrastructure as fully optimized and centralized. Levi said businesses had expected AI to help shrink their software stacks. Instead, they’re dealing with more apps, integrations, and shadow AI usage as employees adopt tools outside their companies’ approved systems. “Managers completed 2025 with the feeling that they will consolidate tools, actually, that they’ll reduce the number of software. But what happened is that the number of tools that they’re using increased,” Levi said. “More than 50% are saying that they’re using more tools now than they did last year, and it’s not stopping.” This need for control seems to be growing urgent as companies deploy AI agents that can act on their own. The survey found that 58% of managers expect to oversee more AI agents than human employees within the next year, and 46% worry about losing control over those agents’ actions. There’s also quite a bit of fear over being held responsible for decisions made by AI (35% of respondents said so), as LLMs are still largely unpredictable. “They don’t want their agents to be fully autonomous,” Levi said, explaining that managers want people to be involved and consulted by AI when it comes to crucial tasks and decisions. At heart, the report’s findings show that AI adoption is increasingly becoming as much a governance problem as it is an opportunity to raise productivity. A run passes a task when its final submission beats the human reference on every metric the task checks, on every hidden workload. Pass rate counts those passes, but it weighs an easy task like a hard one, and a model that passes everything has nowhere left to climb. \(\theta_m\) is the strength of model \(m\), \(\beta_g\) the difficulty of metric \(g\), and \(u_r\) how well this one run went; it is shared by all of the run’s metrics, which come from the same submission. When strength equals difficulty, the chance is one half, and every unit of strength above it multiplies the odds by \(e\). Metrics that every run beats or misses together count once. results:
Nvidia's GTC Berlin keynote on October 21, 2026, centered on a modular data center system and Europe's AI buildout.

- **DSX POD launch:** Nvidia unveiled a system to speed up AI data center construction. One report says it focuses on compressing deployment timelines to as fast as 14 days. It integrates computing, networking, storage, software, power and cooling into a single AI factory reference design.
- **Cost figures:** Huang put a 1-gigawatt AI factory at about $50 billion, including land, power, shell, compute, networking, storage, power cooling and integration. He said a 1 GW facility could generate about $40 billion in annual revenue. He also said every three months of deployment delay can cost about $10 billion in revenue.
- **European investment:** Nvidia said it invested nearly $10 billion in Europe over the past year and announced 14 startup investments during its European tour. A BigGo Finance table dates a joint declaration of intent with Germany's federal government to October 19, though one source's figure of nearly $10 billion is a combined total of about $8 billion already invested and about $2 billion in new plans.
- **Europe's gigawatt context:** The EU's gigafactory call covers up to seven sites and expects more than €20 billion of private money. Bids close November 12 and winners come in early 2027. Several large projects remain plans, not built capacity.
- **Tension to note:** Coverage of the keynote focused on Europe's lagging AI sector. The Washington Post described Huang urging Europe to act, saying the region currently lacks the massive computing power needed for AI data centers.

I didn't find a new gigawatt-scale European site announcement with named locations and dates in these results, so that detail may need a follow-up search.

Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta Platforms topped Wall Street revenue targets in the third quarter and forecast continued top-line growth, even as billions in legal payments for teen mental health litigation cut its operating margins in half, and massive AI investments pushed free cash flow into negative territory.

The company also said it create a Class C stock share class to help it fund the AI buildout, pay employee stock compensation, and fund acquisitions.

Investors ignored the short-term pain for the potential of a future AI payoff, cheering early signs of traction with the recently released Muse AI agent, sending Meta shares up as much as 5% in after-hours trading on Wednesday.

“Our investments are paying off, the core business is strong, and we’re seeing velocity across the board,” Zuckerberg said in a prepared statement on Wednesday, later adding on the conference call that plans were underway to monetize Muse.

“The average revenue per American user for our existing ‘family of apps’ users is several hundreds of dollars annually, and we expect Muse will reach an even higher level over time due to the amount of commerce that we already see taking place,” Zuckerberg said.

Meta’s third-quarter revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion, above the $63.3 billion analysts expected, according to Visible Alpha consensus from S&P Global Market Intelligence. And the company forecast revenue for the final quarter of the year to range between $73 billion and $76 billion, compared with the $73.75 billion expected by analysts.

But Meta’s operating income of $13 billion was down 37% from the $20.5 billion it posted in the second quarter of 2025 as a result of a $10 billion settlement Meta struck with a group of attorneys general over youth safety. The terms of the settlement will see Meta pay about $18 billion to the states over the next decade, depending on cooperation from TikTok and Google’s YouTube. Without the charge, operating income would have been $22.9 billion and earnings of $7.40 a share, rather than $13 billion and $3.83.

Legal issues may continue to take a bite out of Meta’s results. Hours before Meta announced its Q3 results Wednesday, news broke that a New Mexico judge had ordered the company to pay $25 billion in penalties related to the Cambridge Analytica data privacy scandal. Meta plans to appeal.

Net income in Q3 totaled $9.9 billion, or $3.83 a share, versus $2.7 billion, or $1.05 a share in the year-ago period.

Meta is plowing unprecedented amounts of capital into AI infrastructure and services, joining companies like Alphabet , OpenAI, and Microsoft in a race to develop the most advanced AI models. To continue funding the AI effort, Meta said it would reallocate investments from its money-losing virtual reality business, Reality Labs, and that it would create a new nonvoting class C common stock.

Capital expenditures, which have tech investors on tenterhooks, clocked in at $34.9 billion, compared with $31 billion in the second quarter and $19.4 billion a year ago. Meta slightly tweaked its full year capex guidance to $135 billion to $145 billion, from $130 billion to $145 billion.

Free cash flow, which has been a sore spot for Meta, was negative $2.1 billion, compared with $784 million in the second quarter and $10.6 billion a year ago.

The anatomy of a personal health agent

# Abstract
Large language models are enabling a new generation of health agents, yet their ability to address the diverse needs of individuals in everyday health settings remains underexplored 1 , 2 . Here we developed a comprehensive personal health agent that reasons over multimodal data from consumer wellness devices and medical records to provide personalized health support. Through analysis of web search and health forum queries, together with user-centred research involving end users and health experts, we identified four key user journeys: general health knowledge, personal data interpretation, wellness advice, and symptom assessment. These journeys informed three specialist sub-agents: (1) a data science agent that analyses longitudinal wearable and medical data, incorporating population-level statistics to contextualize numerical insights; (2) a health domain expert agent that integrates personal and contextual data with health knowledge to generate personalized insights; and (3) a health coach agent that synthesizes insights, supports multi-turn interaction and goal setting, applies specified psychological strategies and tracks progress. We integrated these capabilities in the personal health agent, an open-source multi-agent framework for dynamic, personalized health interactions. We evaluated the sub-agents and full system across 11 benchmark tasks using automated and human evaluation, with more than 7,000 annotations and 1,350 h of effort from health experts and end users. This represents the most comprehensive evaluation of a personal health agent thus far and provides a concrete foundation for improving access to high-quality personalized health support more broadly.

# Main
Rapid advancements in large language models (LLMs) have driven transformative changes in health. Current LLMs can support various clinical tasks, such as medical documentation 3 , diagnosis 4 , decision support 5 and drug discovery 6 , 7 , as well as consumer health tools, including virtual health assistants 8 , symptom checkers 9 , digital coaches and advisors 10 , 11 , and clinical examination dialogues 12 .
Wearables add continuous activity, sleep, heart rate variability and other physiological signals 13 , 14 , providing longitudinal context for health support. Recent systems connect these data to LLMs 1 , 2 , 8 , 15 , 16 , 17 , but numerical time-series reasoning remains unreliable 18 . Previous systems either cover narrow fitness or sleep questions without deep numerical analysis 8 , or address broader numerical queries without evaluating health expertise and interactive coaching 2 . A comprehensive system must combine these capabilities while maintaining a coherent interaction 19 . Building on these multifaceted developments and the integrated nature of personal health journeys, we envision that the era of intelligent personal health agents is arriving.
Individual needs for daily health and wellness support are highly diverse 2 , 20 , 21 . We used a user-centred design process spanning end-user queries and discussions, surveys and an expert workshop to cover general wellness, fitness and medical topics. The analysis identified four categories of needs: (1) general health knowledge, (2) personal-data interpretation, (3) wellness advice, and (4) health symptoms (Supplementary Table 1 ). These categories require different capabilities. Personal data questions demand numerical precision and code execution; coaching requires open-ended, empathetic dialogue; and knowledge or symptom questions require factual grounding. Our experiments confirmed that a monolithic LLM architecture struggles to balance these competing objectives. We therefore adopted a modular multi-agent architecture that decouples these technical requirements while preserving a cohesive user experience through orchestration and synthesis of individual sub-agent processes.
Three specialists address these requirements. The data science agent (DS agent) converts personal and population-level time series into quantitative analyses, such as estimating changes in running performance. The domain expert agent (DE agent) interprets wearable data, health knowledge and available medical records (in this study, medical records were limited to blood test results because of protocol-level data access constraints; future work could integrate electronic health records with other modalities), for example, by contextualizing a biomarker value. The health coach agent (HC agent) applies evidence-based strategies such as motivational interviewing 22 to support goal setting, identify barriers and guide behavioural change. Because many requests span these roles, we drew inspiration from multi-agent collaboration strategies, such as voting 23 , 24 , iteration 25 , debate 26 and hierarchical team formation 27 , and built the multi-agent personal health agent (PHA) with an orchestrator to assign work and synthesize the outputs of the agents (Fig. 1a ). Of note, PHA is not intended to supplant human health providers, but to explore the technological frontier of consumer empowerment, envisioning how a unified agent can provide more holistic, actionable health insights.
