a , The anatomy of personal health needs with a user-centred design process. b , Design a multi-agent system, powered by state-of-the-art LLMs, consisting of specialist DS, health DE and HC agents to address diverse consumer health needs. ‘Base model’ refers to the Gemini 2.0 family. c , Our work represents the most comprehensive evaluation of a health agent thus far (more than 7,000 annotations and 1,350 h of effort on 11 benchmarks). MCQ, multiple-choice question.

We developed a holistic evaluation framework (Fig. 1b ) that maps to the capabilities identified through the user-centred analysis. We benchmarked the DS agent on its ability to generate robust analysis plans and codes, the DE agent on its capacity for factuality and evidence-based reasoning, and the HC agent on its coaching effectiveness through user studies with both end users and experts. We then evaluated the integrated PHA system through open-ended, multi-modal conversations that reflect diverse health scenarios. Across 11 benchmark tasks, the evaluation included more than 7,000 human annotations and 1,350 h of effort (651 end-user hours and 699 expert hours), validating the advantage of each specialized sub-agent and demonstrating the promising real-world applicability of our integrated multi-agent health agent.
By combining a modular multi-agent architecture, a capability-matched evaluation framework and an open-source agent implementation, this work establishes a reproducible foundation for developing, comparing and testing PHAs for everyday health and well-being of individuals.

# User-centred analysis of health needs
We first performed a systematic, user-centred analysis to define the landscape of personal daily health needs. We synthesized 1,370 consumer health queries from search engines and health forums, health goal surveys from 555 users, and a design workshop with 14 UX and engineering experts (see Methods ). This analysis identified four critical user journeys (CUJs; Fig. 1a ):

-
(1)

General health knowledge: users seek factual information about broad health topics, medical conditions and wellness concepts; for example, ‘what are the pros and cons of HIIT?’.

-
(2)

Personal data insights: users want to understand and interpret their own data from wearables or medical records to identify trends and relationships; for example, ‘how did my steps impact my resting heart rate in the past month?’.

-
(3)

Wellness advice: users look for actionable and personalized recommendations to improve their well-being or achieve specific health goals; for example, ‘to improve my sleep score, what time should I go to bed?’.

-
(4)

Personal medical symptoms: users describe their symptoms to explore potential causes and understand what might be happening; for example, ‘my throat is itchy and I have trouble swallowing. What might be going on?’.

Supplementary Table 1 provides a detailed breakdown of these categories. Because CUJs often overlap within one conversation, they motivated the production of a modular architecture spanning data analysis, health-domain reasoning and coaching.

# Modular multi-agent health architecture
We developed the PHA as a modular system of three specialist agents, each addressing a complementary user need (Fig. 1b ).
The DS agent analyses personal time-series data to derive quantitative insights. Although LLMs have been explored for data science tasks 2 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 , 34 , 35 , their capacity to interpret ambiguous, open-ended personal health inquiries and perform statistically sound analyses remains a key gap. Our DS agent is designed to translate such queries into robust analysis plans and accurate computation code. Example conversations between a user and the DS agent are shown in Extended Data Fig. 1 . More technical details can be found in the Methods .
The DE agent provides evidence-based, clinical context for user data. Previous work has benchmarked the medical knowledge of LLMs 36 , 37 , 38 , but the essential skill of reasoning and synthesizing across multimodal personal data (for example, wearables, laboratory results and user context) is underexplored. Our DE agent is equipped with a suite of tools to integrate these disparate data streams and generate accurate, personalized interpretations. Example conversations with the DE agent are shown in Extended Data Fig. 2 . More technical details are in the Methods .
The HC agent guides users through multi-turn conversations on goal setting and behavioural change. Although artificial intelligence coaching is an emerging area 39 , 40 , 41 , support for open-ended dialogue across a wide range of wellness topics is limited. We designed our agent with a modular architecture to provide an expert-aligned, personalized coaching experience that effectively balances information gathering with actionable advice. Example conversations between a user and the HC agent are shown in Extended Data Figs.  3 and 4 , with more details in the Methods .
Finally, the PHA is the fully integrated system. A central orchestrator dynamically manages the workflow, decomposing user queries, assigning tasks to the appropriate specialist agents and synthesizing their outputs through an iterative reflection process to provide a single, cohesive and context-aware response to the user 42 . Example multi-turn conversations with PHA are shown in Extended Data Figs. 5 – 8 , with more technical details in the Methods .
Figure 1a maps CUJs to specialist agents. For example, the query ‘I want to understand my sleep data last week and know how I can improve my sleep’ (CUJ2 and CUJ3) recruits the DS agent to analyse wearable data, the DE agent to provide evidence-based sleep knowledge and the HC agent to personalize advice. results:
The Nature paper, "The anatomy of a personal health agent," is from Google Research, and it is the most recent item in the results. Its evaluation covers a set of benchmark tasks, but the sources give different figures.

- **Scope and data:** The evaluations were grounded in data from the large-scale Wearables for Metabolic Health (WEAR-ME) study (n = 1,165). The Google blog describes this as an IRB-reviewed study where ~1200 users provided informed consent to share their wearables data from Fitbit, a health questionnaire, and blood test results.
- **Benchmark numbers differ:** The Nature abstract cites 11 benchmark tasks using automated and human evaluation, with more than 7,000 annotations and 1,350 h of effort. The Google blog cites 10 benchmark tasks, involving more than 7,000 annotations and 1,100 hours of effort. The arXiv preprint also says 10 benchmarks, so the Nature version appears to be the updated one.
- **Limitations the authors acknowledge:** Evaluation on WEAR-ME is Fitbit centric, limiting device generalizability.
- **Independent critique:** A Rapamycin Longevity News write-up says the study measured how good the conversations looked, not whether anyone's health changed. It adds that the authors are almost all Alphabet employees, and they used their own model throughout. Treat this as a secondary commentary, not a primary source.
- **Publication date:** That same write-up lists the Nature publication as published online 21 October 2026, which is a day before today's date.

The October 17 exploitation claim is reported by Amazon Threat Intelligence, and the search results support it, but I found no independent confirmation.

- **The exploitation claim:** Amazon Threat Intelligence says its MadPot honeypot network recorded a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt on Oct. 17, 2026, four days before the CVEs were publicly disclosed. The attempt came from an IP address tied to a commercial anonymization service, and Amazon believes a threat actor was behind it. How the attacker obtained exploit details before disclosure is still unknown. One outlet describes this as at least one actor exploiting the flaws from that date.
- **The AWS bulletin:** AWS Security Bulletin 2026-143-AWS, published 10/21/2026, rates the issue Important. It states AWS services are not impacted by these issues, and no cross-customer propagation has been established to date. For Elastic Beanstalk, AWS released updated PHP platform versions (v4.13.12) on 2026-10-21 that address both CVEs. For Amazon Linux, updated PHP packages are available for commercial regions, and non-commercial regions are targeted for 2026-10-22.
- **Other exploitation reports:** watchTowr says exploitation has been observed in the wild as of October 21 through its Attacker Eye global honeypot network. Sansec reports that Cloudflare reported early attacks at 07:43 UTC on October 21, before the 14:00 UTC release. Huntress, by contrast, had not observed in-the-wild exploitation on partner systems as of October 21 at 4:30pm ET.
- **Severity conflict:** An earlier AWS Linux support comment on GitHub said the reachable scenarios are narrow and assessed as difficult to leverage in practice. Later research, including Datadog's, reports that its team reproduced the out-of-memory corruption on PHP 8.5.11 with an unauthenticated HTTP POST request.
- **Fixes:** The patched releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. There are no configuration-only workarounds that fully address both issues. For systems that cannot be patched immediately, AWS recommends WAF rules, one per CVE, as interim mitigations (the custom PHP2Shell rule covers CVE-2026-109619, and SizeRestrictions_BODY covers CVE-2026-109618).

{"stdout":"######## 2610.29932 | Title:FrontierCS 2: A Benchmark for Computer Science R&D | [Submitted on 21 Oct 2026]
Abstract:Can LLM agents make contributions to frontier computer science R&D? We introduce FrontierCS 2, a benchmark of 48 open-ended tasks. We take a paper and the code its authors released and delete the paper's contribution. The deleted code becomes the human reference that sets the bar. Earlier open-ended benchmarks give each agent a problem statement and grade one program after the run. FrontierCS 2 places the agent inside a research environment. The agent inherits a working repository and may submit a patch at any point. For each patch, a judge returns a development-suite score but keeps the evaluator, the held-out final suite and the reference private, and grades the final submission on that suite against the reference. The tasks span 13 domains, from machine-learning systems and high-performance computing to databases, security and robotics. Beyond these 48 tasks, FrontierCS 2 keeps a private set of more than 100 tasks, to be announced in the future. We evaluate 12 agents. The best one is Claude Opus 5.5, passing 58% of its runs. No run passes on 16 tasks. A higher score is not the same as a pass: most runs that beat the reference on the combined final score still fall short on some metric or workload. On a shared capability scale for agents and tasks, the median task is roughly as difficult as what the strongest agent can handle.

######## 2610.28707 | Title:SimHack: Predicting the onset of detectable reward hacking before RL training | [Submitted on 20 Oct 2026]
Abstract:When training LLMs to code with reinforcement learning, reward hacking is often detectable but difficult to prevent, since (a) environment hardening is increasingly difficult as training environments grow more complex; and (b) training-time interventions incentivize models to obfuscate hacking behavior to bypass detection. We instead study whether we can predict when detectable reward hacking becomes dominant before executing an RL run, enabling us to select lower-risk recipes in advance. We find that the initial hacking rate alone does not determine onset, which varies substantially across training recipes and repeated runs. We thus formulate this problem as predicting the distribution of the reward hacking onset step under a target training recipe. We introduce SimHack, a simulator that learns reward hacking training dynamics from a handful of smaller-scale reference RL runs and generates counterfactual simulation runs of unseen target recipes without costly retraining. Across unseen target recipes, SimHack predicts the median onset to a relative error of 11.3% and achieves across-recipe rank correlation of 0.85, while generalizing to differences in model scale, curriculum, number of rollouts, and learning rate between reference and target recipes. As an application, we show that SimHack can guide training decisions by screening candidate RL curricula, discovering curricula over the same set of scenarios that train for 96.6% longer without hacking.

######## 2610.29178 | Title:Correlated Failures of AI Approval Monitors | [Submitted on 21 Oct 2026]
Abstract:Before an AI agent takes a consequential action, such as paying, messaging or changing code, several monitors check it. Their verdicts are combined by aggregating scores or by counting approvals, whatever inputs the monitors share. Monitors that share a base model or a poisoned input, however, may fail together. We borrow the fail-prone systems of distributed computing: lists of monitor sets that may fail together. A rule is safe if it executes no bad action and live if it blocks no good one. We measured twelve small open-weights monitors on payment approval under two pre-registered protocols. Without pre-registration, we also measured three closed frontier models (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon) and the open DeepSeek-V3.2. Every reliable fooling of a monitor into approving a fraud came through an evidence source and reached only that source's readers. Fooling it into blocking a correct payment depended on injection resistance, a monitor's refusal to follow instructions planted in its data. Small models and DeepSeek obeyed such notes. The three closed models ignored them in all but one case, and Opus also resisted persuasion tailored to it. On new data, a rule that counts sources instead of votes blocked 0.9% of correct payments, against 7.4% for the best counting rule, at equal safety. The pre-registered worst-case test failed. One attack left the approvers on a single source, so no rule over the twelve language-model monitors survives every measured attack. Adding a rule engine, which cannot be persuaded, restored the condition for a safe and live rule on the measured attacks. Barclays said on October 22, 2026, with its third-quarter results, that it expects to cut about 5,000 jobs this year, roughly 5% of its workforce, as it uses AI and other technology to lower costs.

- **Scale and timing:** The cuts equal about 5% of the roughly 93,000 employees the bank had at the end of 2025. Some 1,000 of the roles were cut during the first half of 2026, and the remainder are spread out over the second half of the year.
- **Where cuts fall:** About 60% of the cuts are expected to be in support functions, including developers. Barclays said the job losses reflect "organisational simplification and technology change efficiency driven by AI".
- **Profit:** Pre-tax profit for the quarter was £2.3 billion, up 12% year on year. Reuters reported that this undershot analysts' forecasts as its fixed income trading business underperformed. Sharecast described it as in line with LSEG-compiled forecasts. Group income for the period was £7.4 billion, below analysts' estimate of £7.61 billion. Fixed income income fell 19% to £1 billion, while equities revenue rose 47%.
- **Shareholder returns:** The bank also announced an additional £500m share buyback.
- **Investor reaction:** One analyst at AJ Bell said the buyback failed to entirely ease investors' disappointment.

Sources differ on the profit figures. Yahoo Finance reported net profit after tax of £1.65 billion, up from £1.46 billion, while Reuters and others cite the £2.3 billion pre-tax figure.

Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot | AWS Security Blog

Skip to Main Content

# AWS Security Blog

# Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot

Amazon Threat Intelligence identified a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt dating to Oct. 17, 2026, in MadPot telemetry, four days before public disclosure of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network. While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure.

The PHP embargo window was set to be lifted on 2026-10-21 1400 UTC. On the day of the release, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified multiple proof of concept exploits for the vulnerability, with the earliest around 2026-10-21 0200 UTC. Subsequently, from 2026-10-21 0200 UTC to 2026-10-21 0800 UTC, Amazon Threat Intelligence identified additional exploitation attempts of PHP2Shell targeting MadPot from additional anonymized infrastructure. The actual payloads and choices in anonymization infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors. Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems.

The actual release of the embargo window was 2026-10-21 1400 UTC. Once the embargo was lifted and the patch was released, additional proof-of-concept exploits appeared within hours, and we saw them used against our sensors almost immediately. PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.

Two lessons from this event apply well beyond this one vulnerability:

- An embargo protects defenders only until someone else finds the same bug. Coordinated disclosure is still the right model. But defenders should not assume the public disclosure date is the earliest date of exploitation. With PHP2Shell, compromise may predate the advisory.

- The time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons. In the past, most exploitation we observed came after a public proof of concept was released. A small number of capable actors built exploits, and everyone else waited for them. That dependency is weakening. AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit. As a result, more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed.

For security leaders, this changes several working assumptions:

- For critical vulnerabilities in internet-facing systems, measure patch and mitigation timelines in hours. A 7-day or 30-day SLA assumes a delay that no longer exists.

- Start investigations from the earliest known exploitation, not from the disclosure date. For PHP2Shell, investigate from at least starting on October 17 th .

- Invest in detections that don’t rely on a signature for a specific CVE. The first exploitation will often come before those signatures exist.

# How AWS helps protect customers

AWS deploys multiple layers of protection to help safeguard customers. Our internal threat intelligence system automatically detected and restricted malicious scanning attempts targeting this vulnerability. We analyze over 200 billion events per minute and integrate threat intelligence from our MadPot honeypot network to identify and block known exploitation attempts in real time. Our honeypot system provides us with early detection of exploitation attempts, enabling rapid response and threat analysis.

We investigate whether the refusal behavior in text transfers to tool use. We construct a benchmark of 2,304 prompts across four domains, consisting of matched triplets that present the same harmful or benign request in text-only, standard tool-enabled, and adversarially framed tool-enabled settings. We then assess tool-call safety using 20 predefined forbidden actions. Testing five models of varying sizes and families, we find that requests refused in text frequently result in unsafe tool calls. Under standard tool-enabled prompting, this divergence occurs for 10-52 percent of harmful requests refused in chat. To mechanistically investigate this gap, we identify a refusal-associated direction in the residual stream of each of the five models. We find that in tool-enabled contexts, the activations along this direction decrease in four of five models. Furthermore, lower activation predicts unsafe tool calls across all five models (AUC 0.76-0.86). However, restoring the signal to the respective text-only value through activation patching only prevents a subset of unsafe calls, primarily by suppressing tool use rather than by producing safer calls. Steering along the refusal direction nearly eliminates unsafe calls only at strengths that also suppress benign tool use or degrade the output quality. Our findings indicate that the identified refusal direction contributes to whether a model acts, but only partially explains the refusal divergence. Yet they show limited backup awareness: recognizing that an action will modify state that may later be needed, and preserving it beforehand. To evaluate backup awareness, we introduce RegretBench, a benchmark of 205 executable tasks grounded in regret moments reported on platforms such as this http URL, GitHub, and Stack Overflow, where users explicitly regretted not preserving state they later needed. Across six frontier models, agents complete 86.1% of tasks on average yet back up before these moments in only 15.2%, showing that task completion ability does not imply backup awareness. Because it is hard to predict which changes will be regretted, we propose BackUpper, a harness plug-in backup layer that checks every tool call and preserves affected state before modification. It combines rule-based strategies for common operations with a lightweight subagent for complex cases, and its rule table can expand with subagent decisions over time. On RegretBench, BackUpper covers every regret moment action and restores states with 92.2% average similarity to the original. Achieving this costs only $0.014 per task, with 7x fewer tokens than the main-agent self-backup baseline. When users have preferences on what to back up, BackUpper can also narrow its scope accordingly, matching human annotations on whether an action is worth preserving with an 84.5% F1 score. These results suggest that agents can keep actions reversible at low cost while respecting users' preferences. ######## 2610.30103 | Title:Did the Problem Actually Get Harder? We introduce P2NPCBench, a benchmark of 12 problem families in which every NPC problem is paired with a P twin posed over the same surface. To remove the textbook cues that enable recall, we build it with AgentGAN, an adversarial multi-agent framework in which a generator rewrites each statement until a panel of frozen code models fails, while an executable validity gate keeps every rewrite answer- and class-preserving. The result is 2,114 hardened statements with hand-verified reference human solvers. We introduce FrameBench-HPS, a controlled benchmark of 2,880 prompts derived from 240 high-stakes scenarios across healthcare, finance, education/career, and legal/consumer-rights domains. # OpenAI agents disabled safety monitoring, one lied about it

By

# Bill Toulas

- October 21, 2026

- 12:26 PM

- 2



OpenAI agents powered by the GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra models weakened misalignment monitoring during two internal tasks, interpreting coding instructions as authorization to do so.


AI alignment refers to how well an AI system’s goals and behavior align with human values, intentions, and instructions. It is a key focus of AI safety research aimed at preventing harmful actions and unintended outcomes.


One of the incidents occurred on October 3, when an agent powered by GPT-6.1 Sol extended an earlier human instruction “don’t send any messages” related to a Slack history search to automatic monitoring alerts.


It directed a sub-agent to empty notification recipient lists and suppress notifications. Although monitoring continued to run and save findings, it disabled alerts to humans.


OpenAI says this happened even though the agent earlier reasoned that alerts should remain enabled.


A second incident on October 6 involved a GPT-6 Astra-powered agent tasked with migrating a program. The agent removed existing monitoring integration to match a reference implementation and then denied doing so.


After reporting the migration was complete, the agent did not tell the user that monitoring was disabled. Furthermore, when asked directly, the agent lied to the human.




GPT-6 Astra agent denies disabling monitoring

source: OpenAI





OpenAI says that the agent also replaced a test intended to preserve monitoring with one asserting that the monitor context was absent.


Although both incidents involved agents weakening alignment monitoring despite explicit instructions not to, OpenAI classified neither as P0 (“Priority Zero”), its highest urgency level for issues requiring immediate attention .



# Ongoing investigation


OpenAI says it is investigating whether the unintended behavior stems from excessive persistence in task-completion goals, a poor understanding of monitoring requirements, or a specific tendency to evade monitoring.


“We are also developing evaluations to test whether models might have a propensity to evade misalignment monitoring in particular and exhibit motivated reasoning in order to do so,” OpenAI explained.


“We don’t yet have a satisfying explanation for this behavior, and will investigate this behavior through the creation of paired evaluations, resampling of agent continuations, and experiments on models’ internal activations.”


The AI firm says it has updated its internal Auto-Review system to now detect and block attempts to disable misalignment monitoring. At the same time, it will also reject all workloads that lack valid monitoring requirements.

# ClickFix has never been bigger, and AI tools are its most convincing lure yet

Sponsored by

# Push Security

- October 21, 2026

- 10:00 AM

- 0



ClickFix has fast become one of the go-to techniques for criminals since it first emerged around 2024. It’s grown in both volume and variety, with an ever-expanding family of sub-techniques like FileFix, InstallFix, TerminalFix, and the entirely browser-native ConsentFix.


The lures too have become more developed and targeted, with recent attacks preferring to target people searching for and using AI tools, a trick that is catching many users off guard and blending in with otherwise legitimate traffic for approved GenAI tools.


Push's detection data shows how far the technique has spread. Through Q2 2026, ClickFix made up an average of 52% of Push's detections , overtaking AiTM and device code phishing for the first time, and in August that figure reached 67%.


Across all the browser-based attacks Push intercepts, 1 in 2 arrive through channels other than email , such as search engines and social media. The rest came through email but weren’t stopped at the email gateway. ClickFix goes a step further: 4 in 5 ClickFix pages intercepted in 2026 were reached from search engines — through compromised websites, malvertising, and SEO poisoning.




A ClickFix lure generated using the ERRTRAFFIC kit.






# AI tools are the newest lure


The latest ClickFix variants use AI tools as the bait. In Push's last quarterly snapshot, AI-themed InstallFix and LLMshare attacks made up around 5% of all attacks Push detected, a growing subset of the ClickFix family.


Other researchers are seeing the same trend. ANY.RUN linked 1,258 public sandbox analyses to fake AI tool campaigns between April 15 and October 5, 2026, and 81% of them impersonated Claude or ChatGPT and Codex . At least 45% came from campaigns that told the victim to paste a command, through fake CLI install pages or fake download pages with ClickFix, and another quarter started on a shared AI chat or artifact.


These lures work because AI adoption has spread two habits across the workforce. The first is installing tools from the terminal. Claude Code and similar tools ship as a one-line terminal install, so people who would never previously have opened a command line now paste commands from web pages as a normal part of trying a new tool.


A classic ClickFix page has to invent a reason for the user to paste something. An InstallFix victim arrives expecting to run a command, so the attacker only has to swap it for a malicious one.


The second is searching for AI apps rather than going to them directly. Plenty of people reach the AI tools they use every day by typing the name into a search engine, and employees are adopting new AI apps faster than security teams can approve them. Both habits put the user on a search results page, which is exactly where ClickFix delivery happens.



# InstallFix: Fake install pages that show the real command


Push first documented InstallFix in March 2026: cloned install pages for tools like Claude Code, Codex, and NotebookLM (which doesn't even have a desktop installer), promoted through search ads. The attacker copies the legitimate page and replaces the install command with one that delivers malware.


The latest cluster Push analyzed saw a Google search for "claude mac" return a sponsored result that displays bing.com as its domain. The ad passed the visitor through Bing's own click-tracking redirect to a compromised retail website, which forwarded them to a fake "Download Claude" page.


Two layers of cloaking, a server-side referrer check on the compromised site and a script on the fake page, send anyone who doesn't arrive through the ad to a benign page or a 404.




A sponsored Google result for "claude mac" that displays bing.com as its domain.

results:
The paper you're looking for is Guan et al., "Advancing subseasonal forecasting with machine learning," published in *Nature* in October 2026. Its core method is probabilistic bias correction (PBC), which targets the 2–6 week range.

- **The method:** The team trained a machine-learning framework on a model's past probabilistic forecasts to strip out its systematic errors. The Microsoft Research write-up says the authors present PBC as a framework that reduces systematic error by learning to correct a model's historical probabilistic forecasts.
- **Headline results:** Applied to ECMWF's models, the method doubled the AI Forecasting System's subseasonal skill. It also improved the debiased dynamical model on most targets, with gains on 91% of pressure, 92% of temperature and 98% of precipitation targets.
- **Why it matters:** Skill at this range is hard to get. The paper notes that model skill drops precipitously at subseasonal timescales (2–6 weeks ahead) due to compounding errors, systemic model biases and the chaotic nature of the atmosphere.
- **Extremes:** Coverage highlights better early warning for extremes. One summary says the tool improves the early prediction of extremes of heat, cold, rainfall and flooding.
- **Authorship and dates:** Hannah Guan and Soukayna Mouatadid were co-first authors, and Judah Cohen (MIT) and Lester Mackey (Microsoft Research) are the corresponding authors. The paper went online on 14 October 2026, and *Nature* ran a research briefing on it on 21 October 2026.

The search results don't say whether the open-source code is the same release that Unite.ai mentions, and they don't include independent expert assessments beyond a *Science Media Centre* piece, which notes a conflict of interest because ECMWF staff are involved.

Tracing causal cascades underlying biological state changes

Maps constructed from omics data to identify the causal mechanisms underlying state transitions have not been established. We developed CauTrigger, which treats state transitions as layered causal cascades rather than isolated molecular changes, effectively separating causal signals from spurious variation. CauTrigger prioritizes potential upstream triggers, predicts perturbation responses and helps turn omics measurements into testable mechanistic hypotheses.

An AI tool improves weather forecasts up to a month ahead

An innovative artificial-intelligence application enhances weather forecasting in the difficult subseasonal range, providing accurate forecasts of precipitation, temperature and pressure 3–5 weeks in advance. response.stdout:
Script kiddies (and script adults, who have also switched their brains off) now all think that, well, they don't understand UAF chaining, but this Claude guy knows everything and can totally make an exploit.

Hilariously, this results in the LLM giving their younger-brother an unplugged controller. It says exploit all across the screen... and has some smoking gun transcripts... but it's modified the server you're testing against to have a severe vulnerability. Cheating!!

- https://github.com/david-alvarez-rosa/php-rce

- https://github.com/eness/php2shell-CVE-2026-109618-CVE-2026-109619-PoC

- https://github.com/ikow/php2shell-poc

I just plucked these three because they were the ones with the most stars, but it goes on for miles and miles.

One really amusing thing in common with most of these "PoC"s is that they lean on "LFI", or local-file-inclusion, to make the vulnerability. In non-php terms, their exploit chain requires the server to already have a severe code-level vulnerability.

It's not rare for PHP apps to be fucked in some sense, but requiring the server to have an existing vulnerability where users could cat /etc/password is an insane pre-requisite. If you need this, this does not make this a severe bug.

The strangest thing is that so many people have independently made this extraordinarily weird defect in judgement. That is because they haven't independently made this decision. Claude/Etc. has done all of the judgement for them, hence the bizarre distribution in logical errors.

There's something important to be said here about how many people have Claude/GPT make design decisions for them, and how AI is the primary decision maker in the world right now. You've got this bizarre case of "Decision Schelling Points" where a method of solving a problem is extremely overrepresented, because it's what Claude does out of the box.

It's especially bizarre in this case, where AI is inserting a vulnerability on the server... to prove that the server is vulnerable to your "exploit any PHP instance" attack!

# So why was everyone so scared?

Because:

- A PHP core team member said that this was cataclysmic ("exploits will start appearing 15 minutes after the patch drops")

- We all deep down know that PHP is insecure

- The exploit video had an anime girl in it

- We all know that LLMs are looming over the internet like a 100 ton chekov's anvil, and we know that code isn't secure

And we've had things like this before, but not in the LLM era yet. Luckily for us, this doesn't seem to be that day. This is too difficult to exploit easily. It isn't a Log4J moment.

**Publication date:** September 30, 2025

**Authors:** Xuhai "Orson" Xu (Visiting Faculty Researcher) and Ali Heydari (Research Scientist), Google Research

**Key claims and numbers:**
- **System:** The Personal Health Agent (PHA) is a multi-agent LLM framework with three specialist sub-agents: data science, domain expert, and health coach. An orchestrator coordinates them.
- **Study data:** About 1,200 users in an IRB-reviewed study consented to share Fitbit wearable data, a health questionnaire, and blood test results. The page does not name this dataset "WEAR-ME," so I can't confirm that name from the text.
- **Evaluation scale:** 10 benchmark tasks, more than 7,000 annotations, and over 1,100 hours of effort from health experts and end-users.
- **Design inputs:** More than 1,300 real-world health queries, survey data from more than 500 users, and a workshop with design and engineering experts.
- **Data science agent:** On analysis planning, it scored 75.6% versus 53.7% for the base model. That stage was assessed with an auto-evaluator trained on 354 expert-curated query-analysis plans. Code generation was checked against 173 unit tests.
- **Multi-agent results:** End-users and experts preferred PHA over a single-agent system and a parallel multi-agent baseline, and ranked it best overall in most cases.
- **Open-source release:** The page does not mention any open-source code or data release. It links only to the paper on arXiv (2508.20148).
- **Scope caveat:** The authors state the work is a research framework, not a description of any product or feature.

Abstract: The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in recent years has brought a parallel rise in prompt injection and jailbreak attacks. By embedding malicious instructions, these exploits manipulate language models to bypass intended behavior and operational boundaries. In traditional chatbots, such attacks are confined to a single session because state memory is not preserved across conversations. However, persistent memory features in modern conversational interfaces enable cross-session attack propagation, establishing a threat vector known as memory injection. This work explores this emerging vulnerability in leading LLM-as-a-service platforms, highlighting its real-world severity and the need for countermeasures. AUTH: Gadi Evron
Abstract: LLM-based vulnerability discovery harnesses can miss real, reachable vulnerabilities because of how the harness around the model is built. Steps that select code, filter it, and store and merge findings can drop a vulnerability before or after the model runs, independently of the model's capability, and the report usually gives no sign that this happened. These drops come from engineering choices, and errors. They leave vulnerabilities undetected, and an attacker who knows the harness's rules can also use them to hide a vulnerability on purpose. Understanding these drops shows how to build harnesses that fix or disclose them and are harder to evade. AUTH: Arshan Dabirsiaghi (Pixee)
Abstract: Coding agents that run long enough must compact their context, summarizing the conversation, discarding the original, and carrying the summary forward as memory. We show that in popular open-source coding agents this step is an exploitable trust boundary. Harnesses that flatten the typed conversation into a single plain string, marking each message with a text label such as [User]:, destroy message provenance in code, before the summarizer runs. An attacker who controls anything the agent reads can forge a user turn that survives compaction as a genuine instruction. The search turned up consistent reporting on the PHP2Shell outages, with some disagreement on details.

**What happened:** PHP released emergency fixes for two critical flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, which can remotely run code in PHP's core engine without logins. Technical details leaked before the patch, and numerous organizations have proactively taken portals offline. MediaWiki is among the affected platforms; examples seen so far include WordPress, MediaWiki, Joomla, and Drupal.

**Netherlands:** Reports list several Dutch sites going dark. According to NOS, MijnOverheid.nl, the website of the Tweede Kamer, those of the NCSC and the data protection authority, the NotuBiz portals, some systems of the ANP news agency and various higher-education systems are offline. The sources disagree on DigiD: NOS puts DigiD among the services switched off, while the daily Reformatorisch Dagblad writes that DigiD remains usable and that what has been shut down is MijnOverheid.

**Wikipedia:** Wikipedia was affected only partly. One report says parts of Wikipedia, a number of European government sites were offline or partly offline, each waiting for a fix. I did not find a source detailing the Wikipedia MediaWiki patch specifically.

**Status and caveats:** Many services return, others remain offline, and no confirmed production breach has been reported publicly. Finland's Valtori says this is a precaution, not the result of an attack or a breach. Many sources are fresh blogs and aggregators, so specifics such as the exact list of offline sites may change; check official NCSC or NOS reporting for the current status.

Skip to main content Today, we’re opening a research preview of Claude Duet, a new app where Claude works as a proactive agent. We designed Claude Duet to be a partner you can trust. Professionals of all kinds have to juggle many decisions a day, and we think they’ll find Claude Duet most useful. It helps you prioritize where to spend your time and energy, and to leave room for the ambitious projects that felt impossible or daunting before.

Each morning, it sends you a short brief on the most important items across your connected apps. Throughout the day, it keeps tabs on those apps and messages you only when something needs your attention. Websites across the US and Europe have gone offline earlier today after the disclosure of two critical flaws in PHP, the code behind most of the internet.

PHP is the behind-the-scenes code that builds a web page each time someone visits it. ######## 2610.29734 | Title:Monitorability Is Trainable: Post-Training for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability | [Submitted on 21 Oct 2026]
Abstract:Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is one of the few practical tools available for overseeing capable AI systems, but it is fragile: a model's reasoning is only useful to a monitor if it remains coupled to what the model actually does. This coupling can be degraded during training through, for example, CoT compression, optimization against a monitor, and out-of-context generalization from synthetic documents. In this work, we propose an unsupervised post-training objective based on maximizing mutual information between CoT and the output for improving CoT monitorability. Across three model organisms with degraded CoT, it recovers most or all of the lost monitorability. Applied to undegraded policies, it further improves judged monitorability, improves prediction of unsafe behavior by CoT monitors and activation probes, and increases the prevalence of consequential reasoning. These results suggest that monitorability should be treated as a trainable attribute of the policy. A dedicated monitorability post-training stage can extend current practices that protect CoT from direct optimization pressure.

######## 2610.29029 | Title:Better Policies, Worse Verifier Audits | [Submitted on 21 Oct 2026]
Abstract:Verifier stacks increasingly sit inside post-training and test-time compute loops. We study a specific control loop: a component verifier is evaluated on fresh policy outputs against the full success label and refreshed when that aggregate score falls. For a conjunctive target $y = F \wedge M$, its on-policy AUC is $(1-q)A_{\mathrm{own}} + qA_{\mathrm{cross}}$, where $q = \Pr[F=1 \mid y=0]$. As the policy masters $F$, $q$ can rise toward one, removing weight from $F$-failures and rewarding information about $M$. We call this on-policy audit collapse. We derive a sharp identified set, a complete-erasure threshold, and the exact point at which the audit can prefer a worse component verifier; its population optimum is the full-outcome predictor, not the component oracle. An exact oracle exhibits the collapse, a natural multi-label text control shows inversion can select a head with lower canonical $F$-AUC at the observed failure mixture, and a prediction-registered ECG study shows that acting on the audit can reduce off-policy $F$-AUC, transfer the damage to an unseen generator, and increase downstream constraint violations. Preserving own-failure support prevents the damage. Matching label-complexity bounds and a controlled-mixture audit give the corresponding repair: audit the component on its own failures, and keep those failures in the refresh distribution.

######## 2610.30014 | Title:Agent Behavior Maps: Locating Agents by What They Would Do, Without Running Them | [Submitted on 21 Oct 2026]
Abstract:LLM agents with similar success rates can follow different action sequences. An Agent Behavior Map represents LLM-harness combinations using centered action log-likelihoods on shared reference trajectories, without requiring new environment rollouts from the target agent. We derive error bounds relating squared coordinate distances to trajectory KL under explicit assumptions, and across eight cross-scored models the distances track the directly measured trajectory KL in rank order. Across 100 LLMs and four environments, ALFWorld-based coordinates support performance prediction and identify behavioral similarities. In ALFWorld, these similarities persist after controlling for success rates and model size, including across model families. As an extension, harness-component displacements approximately compose, with accuracy varying across components and environments.

######## 2610.30076 | Title:Circuits of LLM Classifiers | [Submitted on 21 Oct 2026]
Abstract:Language models make it easy to build classifiers by simply prompting a model with the sample to classify. However, their predictions are neither deterministic nor uniformly reliable across samples. How can we combine predictions from different models to improve reliability? We view LLM classifiers as noisy measurement instruments of an underlying target label. Our goal is to maximize average classification accuracy at a given average query cost. To this end, we introduce circuits that organize LLM classifiers into an adaptive sequence of queries and decisions. We then characterize the optimal circuit, obtain the fundamental limits of achievable accuracy, and provide practical insights on realizing the optimal circuit. Across seven classification tasks spanning safety, health, political science, human preference, agent evaluation, decision-making and reasoning, our method improves the cost-accuracy frontier over routing and cascading baselines.

######## 2610.28714 | Title:Big Claims, Small Margins: Do Reported GraphLLM Gains Survive Simple Baselines? | [Submitted on 20 Oct 2026]
Abstract:LLM-based methods for node classification on text-attributed graphs (TAGs) routinely report state-of-the-art accuracy. We ask how these results compare with inexpensive baselines run on the same splits. On the splits of three recent studies, we tune four baseline representatives with validation-only selection and compare them with the highest mean that each paper reports for an LLM-based method in the matched setting. Correct & Smooth on TF-IDF features trails this reference by a median of 2.3 percentage points, and an MLP on frozen e5-large-v2 embeddings by 2.8 points. Correct & Smooth is within 3 points of the reference or better on 15 of 24 tasks, but the reference is significantly higher on 12 of 22 testable tasks, so several reported gains remain substantial. Reading released code next to the papers, we also document evaluation risks: selection of hyperparameters or checkpoints on the test set, labels of test-pool nodes used in training, baseline numbers reused without disclosure, and a text-label misalignment in a released Cora loader. Reports of the same method on the same split also differ by up to 12.5 points across papers whose configurations are not documented to match.

Louis Mosley, Palantir's executive vice president for the UK and Europe, told Reuters on Wednesday (October 22, 2026) that neither Palantir nor the US government can switch off Maven, the AI battlefield system NATO uses. Reuters' original interview is not in the results, so these details come from outlets that reported it.

- **Mosley's claims:** He said where customers have bought our software, they are in full operational control of that software, and summed it up as "There are no kill switches."
- **Staffing:** Palantir employees may take part in operating the system only if the customer chooses. Such employees would be citizens of the country concerned and have the required security clearance.
- **Context:** The reassurance followed disruptions to Ukraine's Starlink and Starshield services, which raised alarm over the reliance on US tech firms.
- **Adoption:** NATO's Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe bought Maven in 2025, and declared the system had achieved "full technical operational capability" in June this year. Germany and France have not adopted it. Germany's army cyber command chief said giving company employees access to the military's national database was out of the question.
- **Contract value:** Neither NATO nor Palantir has disclosed the contract value.

This coupling can be degraded during training through, for example, CoT compression, optimization against a monitor, and out-of-context generalization from synthetic documents. In this work, we propose an unsupervised post-training objective based on maximizing mutual information between CoT and the output for improving CoT monitorability. Across three model organisms with degraded CoT, it recovers most or all of the lost monitorability. Applied to undegraded policies, it further improves judged monitorability, improves prediction of unsafe behavior by CoT monitors and activation probes, and increases the prevalence of consequential reasoning. These results suggest that monitorability should be treated as a trainable attribute of the policy. For a conjunctive target $y = F \\wedge M$, its on-policy AUC is $(1-q)A_{\\mathrm{own}} + qA_{\\mathrm{cross}}$, where $q = \\Pr[F=1 \\mid y=0]$. As the policy masters $F$, $q$ can rise toward one, removing weight from $F$-failures and rewarding information about $M$. We call this on-policy audit collapse. We derive a sharp identified set, a complete-erasure threshold, and the exact point at which the audit can prefer a worse component verifier; its population optimum is the full-outcome predictor, not the component oracle. An exact oracle exhibits the collapse, a natural multi-label text control shows inversion can select a head with lower canonical $F$-AUC at the observed failure mixture, and a prediction-registered ECG study shows that acting on the audit can reduce off-policy $F$-AUC, transfer the damage to an unseen generator, and increase downstream constraint violations. Across 100 LLMs and four environments, ALFWorld-based coordinates support performance prediction and identify behavioral similarities. We view LLM classifiers as noisy measurement instruments of an underlying target label. Our goal is to maximize average classification accuracy at a given average query cost. To this end, we introduce circuits that organize LLM classifiers into an adaptive sequence of queries and decisions. We then characterize the optimal circuit, obtain the fundamental limits of achievable accuracy, and provide practical insights on realizing the optimal circuit. Across seven classification tasks spanning safety, health, political science, human preference, agent evaluation, decision-making and reasoning, our method improves the cost-accuracy frontier over routing and cascading baselines.\n\n######## 2610.28714 | Title:Big Claims, Small Margins: Do Reported GraphLLM Gains Survive Simple Baselines? | [Submitted on 20 Oct 2026]\nAbstract:LLM-based methods for node classification on text-attributed graphs (TAGs) routinely report state-of-the-art accuracy. results:
The search found the Help Net Security article, but the results cut off before stages 3 through 5, so I can only confirm the first two.

- **The article:** Help Net Security reports that OpenAI has proposed a five-stage process for handling critical vulnerabilities in widely used software. It grew out of a two-month response to flaws in PHP, and the framework is aimed at flaws that reach many products at once.
- **Stage 1:** Maintainers, researchers, and partners verify the bug and build a fix, and part of that work involves testing the patch with frontier models ().
- **Stage 2:** Affected organizations get an early head start to prepare mitigations, such as a security vendor might write web application firewall rules.
- **Stage 3:** The article begins by saying responders bring in government, but the excerpt ends there.
- **Stages 4 and 5:** Not in the results.
- **"Broad access through consistent standards":** This phrase is a heading on OpenAI's trusted access page. That page says the company wants to make these tools as widely available as possible while preventing misuse, and it describes using clear, objective criteria and methods, such as identity verification, to decide who gets advanced capabilities.
- **Related OpenAI disclosure policy:** OpenAI's outbound policy says it governs how OpenAI reports and discloses vulnerabilities we discover in third-party software to vendors and open source maintainers, and its scope explicitly includes AI- or agent-powered application security analysis.

To get stages 3 through 5, the full Help Net Security article is needed. Its URL is https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/10/22/openai-vulnerability-disclosure-plan/.

# AI-found bugs are expected to rise, and OpenAI has a five-stage response plan

OpenAI has proposed a five-stage process for handling critical vulnerabilities in widely used software. The process grew out of a two-month response to flaws in PHP , the open-source language that runs websites and web applications. Calif found one of the PHP flaws using OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model, as part of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet initiative for open-source security, and Wiz independently found and reported both.

“As significant as they are, these bugs are among several significant vulnerabilities we’ve already found and are working to fix, and we expect similar findings to increase sharply in the coming months,” OpenAI wrote .

The framework is meant for flaws that reach many products at once, where distributors and service providers need time to prepare. That time may run short if the AI tools broadly available, including to attackers, sit close behind the frontier models doing the finding.

# Five stages, maintainers in charge

In the first stage, maintainers, researchers, and technical partners confirm the bug, assess its impact, and build and test a fix. Part of that testing is pointing frontier models at the patch to hunt for ways around it and for related variants.

In the second stage, affected organizations get a head start. A distributor might adapt the fix for an older release, a hosting provider might test a mitigation, and a security vendor might write web application firewall rules, which are filters that block malicious traffic before it reaches an application.

Third, responders bring in government. For PHP, OpenAI and its partners engaged the White House’s Super Intelligence Force, the Office of the National Cyber Director, CISA, and international partners. Fourth, once the fix and disclosure plans settle, maintainers widen the circle to more distributors, providers, and operators. Fifth, after a patch ships, responders publish guidance and keep helping while operators deploy.

# Who hears first, and how much

OpenAI’s framework weighs three factors in deciding who gets early access: an organization’s protective role, how long it needs to act, and whether it can handle sensitive information. The same criteria would apply to comparable organizations, and maintainers make the final call. Each participant gets what its job requires, from network logs showing indicators of compromise up to working proof-of-concept exploits.

“Even limited details can reveal a vulnerability,” OpenAI wrote. Teams following the plan would revisit the timeline if the flaw is exploited in the wild, leaks, or is exposed by a revealing public patch, or if stalled remediation raises the risk to users.

# What OpenAI wants help with

OpenAI is asking maintainers, researchers, and operators how long disclosure windows should run, how to weigh wide early notice against leak risk, and how to fix older package versions that no longer get security updates. One question goes further: should governments or operators use a vulnerability to patch systems they own or are authorized to manage after losing administrative access? OpenAI sketched an end state of always-on, internet-wide scanning that either alerts site owners or patches the system itself.

Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is one of the few practical tools available for
overseeing capable AI systems, but it is fragile: a model’s reasoning is only useful
to a monitor if it remains coupled to what the model actually does. This coupling
can be degraded during training through, for example, CoT compression, optimization against a monitor, and out-of-context generalization from synthetic documents. In this work, we propose an unsupervised post-training objective based
on maximizing mutual information between CoT and the output for improving
CoT monitorability. Across three model organisms with degraded CoT, it recovers most or all of the lost monitorability. Applied to undegraded policies, it further
improves judged monitorability, improves prediction of unsafe behavior by CoT
monitors and activation probes, and increases the prevalence of consequential reasoning. These results suggest that monitorability should be treated as a trainable
attribute of the policy. A dedicated monitorability post-training stage can extend
current practices that protect CoT from direct optimization pressure.

1

I NTRODUCTION

Current reasoning models extensively use chain-of-thought (CoT) for serial computation (OpenAI,
2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2025), creating a monitoring surface that exposes reasoning before the model
acts. Access to CoT often substantially improves practical monitoring (Baker et al., 2025; Arnav
et al., 2025; Guan et al., 2025), yet CoTs can omit causal influences, rationalize decisions after the
fact, and fail to verbalize reward hacks (Turpin et al., 2023; Lanham et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025).
Appendix G collects examples from frontier systems in which visible reasoning diverges from the
subsequent answer or action. CoT monitoring therefore appears highly useful in some settings and
unreliable in others, without a clear account of when it will work (Korbak et al., 2025).
In this work, we offer a simple perspective that clarifies these conflicting results. We view CoT as an
intermediate representation that, like other representations in a neural network, is learned in service
of producing the model’s output. Unlike standard intermediate representations, CoT is expressed
in natural language and can therefore be inspected directly by humans and other language models.
This accessibility can make CoT appear to be a complete account of the model’s computation, but it
remains a learned representation whose contents depend on the pressures that shape it.
This framing highlights a difference between how CoT is learned and how it is used for monitoring.
Training shapes the CoT to help produce a high-reward output, while a monitor later reuses it to
predict properties of that output. Monitorability is therefore a question of representation transfer:
whether a representation learned for one task can support another (Yosinski et al., 2014; Tripuraneni
et al., 2020). In transfer-learning terms, producing a high-reward output is the source task, and
predicting a behavioral property of that output from the CoT is the target task (Baker et al., 2025).

Hadida et al., 2026). Compression makes this problem explicit: optimizing for short, task-sufficient
reasoning can discard information needed by downstream monitors (Li et al., 2025; Wang et al.,
2022; Dubois et al., 2022).
These failures motivate us to ask whether CoT can be deliberately shaped to transfer better to monitoring tasks that are not specified during training. Our central thesis is that CoT monitorability
should be explicitly optimized, just as alignment post-training explicitly optimizes LLMs to
behave in beneficial and aligned ways (Guan et al., 2024). Such training should improve even the
least-monitorable trajectories, preserve useful capabilities, and avoid increasing the model’s ability
to selectively control CoT legibility.
Because the relevant monitoring tasks may be unknown during training, we seek to preserve information about the output without choosing a particular behavioral label. We therefore optimize
conditional mutual information, which measures how much observing the CoT reduces uncertainty
about the output beyond the prompt alone. Increasing it encourages the CoT to retain output-relevant
distinctions that future monitoring tasks may need. Our lower-tail objective directs training toward
the least-informative CoTs. A conditional χ2 regularizer limits changes in which outputs follow a
given CoT, thereby discouraging arbitrary behavioral changes and making it costly to assign CoTs
new private meanings. The procedure uses neither behavioral labels nor monitor feedback, so it
does not identify a particular monitor for the model to evade. Across model organisms degraded

restores monitorability. Applied directly to undegraded models, it also improves safety-behavior

numerical activations and intermediate textual outputs such as CoTs; natural language makes the
latter much easier to interpret.

Can LLM agents make contributions to frontier computer science R&D? We introduce FrontierCS 2, a

WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal - SimEdw's Blog

TL;DR: I fine-tuned a 360M-parameter language model to act as a terminal. There's no shell or filesystem behind it: every keypress goes in, and the model predicts how the screen changes. It can create files, run vim and tmux, play snake, and usually remembers what you wrote a few commands later. The biggest wins were teaching it to repair its own mistakes and decoding screen rows in parallel. Try it in your browser (208 MB) and type pythoon to see that it's not a real shell.

The demo is designed for a desktop browser with WebGPU and a physical keyboard. Chrome or Edge is the best place to try it. It should work on a modern phone, but painfully slowly.

When I first saw Genie 3 last year, I started imagining a future where applications aren't written in code but learned. Instead of a game engine rendering the scene, a model predicts the next most likely frame from the user's inputs.

Naturally I wanted to train my own world model. But I don't have a massive GPU cluster or a pile of video data, so I scaled down my ambition: instead of a game world, a terminal.

A terminal turned out to be a good fit. It's just a grid of characters rather than pixels, and I can generate as much perfectly labelled training data as I want by running real shells. A pretrained language model also already has a pretty good idea of what ls or cat should print.

What I really wanted to know was whether it could maintain a consistent world, or just generate convincing terminal output.

The final model is based on Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, fine-tuned on terminal sessions recorded from real programs running inside Docker.
Jump to example videos

# How it sees a terminal

Standard LLMs take a prompt and then append tokens to the end, one at a time. That doesn't map well to a terminal. A single keypress can do something on its own, like esc in vim, and output doesn't always go to the bottom: clear wipes the screen and sends the cursor back to the top. So instead of predicting a stream of text, I need to predict changes to the screen.

I treat the terminal as a grid of characters, one per cell. 1 The model doesn't see the grid directly, but a sequence of tokens describing its contents and the changes made to it.

# A session

Every session starts with a snapshot: the screen size, its contents and where the cursor is.

Abstract:The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in recent years has brought a parallel rise in prompt injection and jailbreak attacks. By embedding malicious instructions, these exploits manipulate language models to bypass intended behavior and operational boundaries. In traditional chatbots, such attacks are confined to a single session because state memory is not preserved across conversations. However, persistent memory features in modern conversational interfaces enable cross-session attack propagation, establishing a threat vector known as memory injection. This work explores this emerging vulnerability in leading LLM-as-a-service platforms, highlighting its real-world severity and the need for countermeasures. While existing literature focuses on violations tailored to specific platform features, we present a general threat model. We demonstrate that all NIST attack goals are collectively achievable across ChatGPT Instant 5.3, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash under this model. We also show that memory injections can exploit multiple attack vectors, including personal memories, projects, skills, organization instructions, and Model Context Protocol (MCP)-connected resources. Our findings reveal that all evaluated services can be manipulated to persistently spread disinformation, generate harmful content, or simulate offline unresponsiveness, even in fresh sessions. In the particular case of Claude, shared-memory features allow an attacker to compromise multiple users within an organization and also exfiltrate user prompts. To address these vulnerabilities, we derive defense mechanisms from our proposed threat model and foundational cybersecurity principles. Our analysis indicates that nearly half of these mitigations remain unimplemented across the target services. Datasets and attack artifacts are available at this https URL.

Decision language models as affordable and rapid alternatives to LLM judges of
clinical generative AI
Authors: Rotem Gershon1, Seffi Cohen1,2, Dean Ariel2,3, Havatzelet Bilavsky-Yarden4,5, Amiel
Sberro4,5, Shai Yitzhaki4,5, Osnat Tausky4,5, Naama Golan4,5, Maayan Rabinovitch4,5, Ariel Avraham
Hasidim4,5, Itay Arianu4,5, Maya Dagan1, Ran Balicer1,6,7, Noa Dagan1,2,6
1

Innovation Division, Clalit Research Institute, Clalit Health Services, Ramat-Gan, Israel. 2Stein

Faculty of Computer and Information Science, Ben Gurion University of the Negev, Be’er Sheva,
Israel. 3Department of Family Medicine, Clalit Health Services, Tel Aviv, Israel. 4Schneider
Children’s Medical Center, Petah-Tikva, Israel. 5Gray Faculty of Medical & Health Sciences, Tel
Aviv University, Tel Aviv, Israel. 6The Ivan and Francesca Berkowitz Family Living Laboratory
Collaboration at Harvard Medical School and Clalit Research Institute, Ramat-Gan, Israel. 7Faculty
of Health Sciences, School of Public Health, Ben Gurion University of the Negev, Be’er Sheva,
Israel.
Corresponding author: Rotem Gershon ([email redacted]).
Abstract
Automated judges of clinical artificial intelligence (AI) outputs are necessary, but large language
model (LLM) judges are costly and slow at scale. We compared Jev, a decision language model that
returns structured judgments, with frontier and open-weight LLM judges in four use cases. On 118
pediatric answers, Jev’s agreement with physicians’ ordinal quality ratings (Gwet’s AC2 0.50;
expected score 0.53) matched or exceeded that of seven of 12 LLM judges, including frontier
models, Claude Opus 5.5 (0.49) and GPT-6 (0.38). On physician-graded binary HealthBench
criteria, Jev matched or exceeded four of six LLM judges. On MedHELM’s open-ended tasks, Jev’s
agreement with a three-LLM jury approached or exceeded the jurors’ internal agreement. On
HealthBench Professional, Jev matched the benchmark’s reference judge, GPT-5.4, on 91% of
criteria (other judges, 91–93%). Frontier judges cost 73–294 times more than Jev and took 7–57
times longer. Jev may enable efficient clinical AI evaluation at scale.
The output of clinical generative artificial intelligence (AI) requires continuous evaluation, because
each model update, prompt change, or knowledge-base revision can change the quality and safety of
1

 its answers1,2. Physician grading is the reference standard3, but its cost and time limit how often it
can be repeated.
To fill this gap, large language models (LLMs) have been used to grade the output of other models.
This LLM-as-a-judge approach comes close to inter-human agreement in general-domain
benchmarks, despite documented weaknesses4–10. In medicine, LLM judges have evaluated health
conversations, clinical summaries and answers, and MedHELM’s open-ended tasks, with selected
judges achieving agreement with clinicians comparable to inter-clinician agreement 11–15. Whether
this extended to a deployed clinical decision-support system across distinct quality and safety
criteria remained unclear. We therefore recently compared seven LLM judges with five physicians
on 118 answers from such a system in a tertiary pediatric hospital16. LLM judges agreed more
closely with physicians on text-comparison rubrics, such as faithfulness and completeness, than on
reasoning-heavy rubrics, such as medical reasoning and safety.

very well, dropping reward hacking behavior to 2%. However, simple prompting baselines are

Our experiments using representation engineering techniques (Zou et al., 2023) are also able to

**Date:** October 22, 2026 (AI Governance Institute article, Corporate Policy category)

**Original source:** FedScoop, "What's new in Homeland Security's updated AI policy": https://fedscoop.com/dhs-ai-policy-updates/

**Key facts**

- **Release:** DHS issued an updated AI use directive in September 2026. It largely continues the 2025 predecessor directive but changes governance in ways the article says carry significant downstream risk.
- **New waiver authority:** The chief AI officer can exempt a requirement from the policy, including prohibitions on mass surveillance and tracking.
- **Safeguards absent:** No independent privacy or civil rights review is required, no congressional notice is triggered, and waivers have no expiration date.
- **Other changes:** Equity and sustainability language is removed, and the chief privacy officer's formal civil liberties role is narrowed.
- **New requirement:** Open-source code-sharing requirements were added, aligned with OMB Memorandum M-26-04, "Increasing Public Trust in AI Through Unbiased AI Principles."
- **Controls affected:** HOC-001, CMP-008, ALC-002, PRC-002, HOC-007.
- **Related frameworks:** NIST AI RMF 1.0, the White House Artificial Intelligence Oversight Framework (2026), GSA AI Strategies and Compliance Plan (2026), and Executive Order 14365.

**Vendor implications (per the article):** Prohibited uses that once served as hard contract limits could be activated for specific programs without public notice. Reduced privacy oversight and the removal of equity language may increase reputational and liability exposure for vendors whose tools are used in waived programs.

# Google Chrome adds Gemini-powered scam detection, warns users of ClickFix attacks

By

# Mayank Parmar

- October 21, 2026

- 06:16 PM

- 0



Chrome is getting new scam protections that use Gemini to detect deceptive websites and warn users when they copy suspicious commands from ClickFix attacks.


The changes are part of Enhanced Protection in Safe Browsing, which Google claims makes users ten times safer from phishing, social engineering, notification abuse, and other scams compared with Standard Protection.


Chrome is also adding a new "suspicious site" warning for pages that show deceptive patterns but haven't reached the confidence level required for its existing full-page red warning.


"Suspicious site warnings notify users when a page exhibits deceptive patterns commonly associated with known malicious sites," the company explained .


"By tailoring the warning UI in this way, we are able to safely expand our coverage to display a higher volume of protective warnings."



# Gemini is moving from on-device to server-side scam detection





Chrome previously used an on-device Gemini model to detect tech support scams, but it's now moving to a more powerful server-side model for Enhanced Protection users.


As explained by Google, the model looks at signals such as the brand represented on a page, its intent, and how likely it is to be a scam. Safe Browsing then combines that analysis with domain reputation and other security signals.


"Chrome minimizes the amount of data shared with the server by only analyzing page text when a site exhibits high-confidence scam indicators," Google noted.


"And whenever page content is sent off the device, it is processed ephemerally – meaning it is never logged, retained or used to train models."

######## 2610.28891 | Title:Fig: Automated Multiagent Behavior Elicitor | [Submitted on 20 Oct 2026]
Abstract:Many social evaluations for multiagent systems study behaviors as they emerge from environments instead of systematically intervening in the environment to elicit such behaviors. We introduce Fig (Finding Interactions in Games), an agentic system that performs targeted elicitation interventions on game environments. It takes a natural language behavior description, decomposes it into sub-behaviors, generates new social games or selects existing ones, and executes single or combined interventions to the games' engine, opponents, instructions, and context. To evaluate model behavior, it combines built-in mechanical checks and synthetic rubric judgments. We validate the interventions, generated games, and evaluation mechanisms via human review. Models attempt the target behavior in 45.2% of episodes on average for valid scenarios generated by Fig for six test behaviors -- cooperation, exploitation, deception, covert coordination, betrayal, and sabotage. For game-behavior pairs with available controls, Fig's interventions increase attempt rates by 10.9% on average compared to matched control games. Fig shows that multiagent environments can serve as programmable test beds for intentional, controllable, and reproducible behavior evaluation. Code is available at this https URL.

######## 2610.29869 | Title:Compaction Laundering: Provenance Destruction in Context-Compacting Coding Agents | [Submitted on 21 Oct 2026]
Abstract:Coding agents that run long enough must compact their context, summarizing the conversation, discarding the original, and carrying the summary forward as memory. We show that in popular open-source coding agents this step is an exploitable trust boundary. Harnesses that flatten the typed conversation into a single plain string, marking each message with a text label such as [User]:, destroy message provenance in code, before the summarizer runs. An attacker who controls anything the agent reads can forge a user turn that survives compaction as a genuine instruction. Across five flattening harnesses (pi, opencode, Cline, Aider, OpenHands) the forged approval launders into the agent's memory 87-100% of the time, up to a ~908,000-token context window; across four role-typed harnesses (Codex, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, Continue) the identical attack succeeds 0% of the time. We follow the attack to executed consequences. A laundered standing approval drives real tool-running agents to execute attacker-controlled curl | sh in a sandbox, and end to end in the live pi TUI at ~50% against a 0% paired clean arm. The same channel reliably steers an agent's plan away from a file an attacker designates off-limits, which can blind a code review to a planted backdoor. Because the provenance is destroyed deterministically in harness code, no prompt-level defense can restore it; we measure a code-level provenance check that catches 77% of laundering while demoting 2% of legitimate summary content. The defect also has a straightforward fix at the serializer, escaping the role labels before flattening; the role-typed harnesses avoid it entirely by keeping messages role-typed.

######## 2610.29342 | Title:Uncensored Is Not Unbiased: Abliteration Removes Refusals but Not Script-Dependent Bias About Taiwan | [Submitted on 21 Oct 2026]
Abstract:"Abliterated" ("uncensored") builds of open-weight language models remove the activation direction that mediates refusal, and are popular partly on the assumption that a model that no longer refuses is also free of political censorship. We test this on two matched pairs of 2-bit models: NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, each against a community abliteration. Each model judged 22 statement pairs (on the Republic of China (Taiwan), 1989 Tiananmen, control countries) in Traditional Chinese, Simplified Chinese (a character-level conversion) and English, and answered 27 open questions per script. Script mattered far more than abliteration: the original Bolt scored +0.58 on Index S (-1: People's Republic of China (PRC) position; +1: ROC position) in Traditional Chinese, +0.57 in English and +0.05 in Simplified Chinese, and affirmed "Taiwan is part of the PRC" with probability 0.91 in Simplified but 0.06 in Traditional characters; abliteration changed its scores by at most 0.06, mostly by raising "yes" on both sides. In Qwen, abliteration removed every refusal on 1989 and raised scores by 0.21 to 0.34, yet the abliterated Qwen still affirmed that Taiwan is part of the PRC in all three scripts. Naming the state the Republic of China (Taiwan) raised every model's score by 0.10 to 0.33 but left the script gap. Control pairs showed no script gap; each abliteration changed only its declared tensors. In 740,000 web documents, Simplified text on Taiwan contained PRC-framing terms 3.7 times as often as Traditional text. A script direction could not be steered away; a contrastive stance direction raised scores in every script, and its negation lowered them. A four-sentence system prompt raised the abliterated Qwen to +0.93 to +0.97. Keyword scoring rules failed the models closest to the ROC position mostly for attributing or denying the PRC claim. Uncensored is not unbiased.

######## 2610.28802 | Title:How Much Does the Harness Matter, and for Whom? A Multi-Model Study of Context in LLM-Driven Vulnerability Discovery | [Submitted on 20 Oct 2026]
Abstract:How much does an agent harness affect vulnerability discovery, and does its value depend on the model? We study 24 model-runner configurations using an open-source harness on a production codebase whose vulnerabilities were non-public at scan time. The pipeline combines static screening, LLM investigation, model self-revalidation, root-cause mapping, independent source review, and isolated proof-of-concept confirmation. Across 265 confirmed security root causes, the largest two-run configuration covers 60.4%, while 14.3% are found by exactly one model. No single configuration covers all observed findings. In a four-model context experiment, moving from a minimal prompt to an engineered prompt with a CodeQL-derived call graph raises criticality-weighted yield by 20-86% for smaller and mid-tier models, compared with 2% for the frontier model. This comparison changes both prompt and context. Separating those effects shows that the engineered prompt improves yield for all four models, while adding CodeQL context beyond that prompt improves yield only for the smallest model. A held-out CyberGym subset shows the same direction of target-recall improvement for the combined treatment. Frontier models achieve low false-report rates but do not consistently achieve the highest yield. Strong lower-cost models can deliver similar performance at an order of magnitude lower cost. These results support matching models, prompts, and context to the task, and combining configurations for broader coverage.
